POLITICO https://www.politico.eu European Politics, Policy, Government News Tue, 17 Nov 2026 18:04:38 +0000 en hourly 60 https://wordpress.org/?v=6.9.11 The 5 Labour groups that matter as Burnham shows his hand on welfare https://www.politico.eu/article/5-labour-group-matter-andy-burnham-welfare-social-security/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Tue, 17 Nov 2026 18:04:31 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9332436 LONDON — Keir Starmer’s failed attempt at welfare reform was the beginning of the end of his premiership. Andy Burnham needs to avoid a similar fate. 

The new prime minister’s own effort to tackle a rapid surge in working-age sickness and disability benefit claims kicked off in earnest on Tuesday, when former Labour Cabinet minister Alan Milburn published a long-awaited review into youth unemployment — before being given a new post chairing a youth opportunities unit to help drive the reforms.

He proposes changing the disability benefits young people are entitled to while giving them a legal right to education, employment or training. He also suggests that employers’ National Insurance contributions should be cut for 21-to-24-year-olds in the retail and hospitality sectors for five years.

There’s a long way to go before MPs find out which of Milburn’s recommendations the government implements. A white paper and legislation are not due to be published until next year.

Getting Labour MPs — many of whom are long-standing anti-poverty campaigners — to back plans which ultimately aim to cut Britain’s massive welfare bill will be no mean feat.

Despite a huge majority in the House of Commons, Starmer was forced to roll back plans to reduce personal independence payments — which go to disabled people both in and out of work — after a well-organized campaign by senior Labour figures back in 2025.

POLITICO runs through the key figures from the governing party whose views on the report — and critically Burnham’s eventual proposal — are worth paying attention to.

1) The committee chairs 

Treasury Committee Chair Meg Hillier and Work and Pensions Committee Chair Debbie Abrahams played a crucial role in halting some of Starmer’s welfare reforms.  

Hillier wrote an amendment to Starmer’s welfare plans which would have stopped the bill at its first hurdle. More than 100 Labour MPs from across the party signaled they would back it, forcing ministers to change course and promise any changes would only be made after a review by Disabilities Minister Stephen Timms, which is due later this month.

Abrahams — who supported Hillier’s blocking amendment — was another key organizer of the welfare revolt under Starmer, and has repeatedly warned that reform should not take support away from those who need it most. 

Hillier said last week, after some of Milburn’s proposals were previewed in an interview in the Times newspaper, that he had “done some very good work on this” and she was “giving him a fair wind.”

She said it was “quite radical and quite bold and quite right to be looking holistically at the person in the middle of this, not just about the money or the structure of the benefits.”

On Tuesday, Abrahams described them as the “opportunity of a generation,” welcoming Milburn’s “rigorous analysis” on why young people become “NEETs” – not in education, employment or training.

2) The ministers 

Milburn’s proposals come with a price tag, making Chancellor John Healey a crucial figure to watch as Burnham finalizes his plans.

The overall changes would cost £5.8 billion a year — offset by £6 billion in savings, Milburn suggests.

Also sitting around the Cabinet table is Burnham’s de facto deputy, Louise Haigh, who helped organize the rebellion against Starmer’s welfare reforms.

And Vicky Foxcroft, who quit as a government whip in June 2025, warning that cuts to PIP and Universal Credit should “not be part of the solution” to bringing down the welfare bill, is now a culture minister.  

All are now bound by collective responsibility, where ministers must not speak out openly against the government agenda. 

But every word they utter on welfare will be closely scrutinized for clues on exactly where the government might land.

3) The grandee 

Former Prime Minister Gordon Brown — who has long campaigned against poverty and inequality — is seen as an authority on welfare in the Labour Party.

He parked the convention that ex-prime ministers try not to make life difficult for their successors in an interview with the New Statesman last year, reflecting on the “worrying issue” of reducing social security that left people “in poverty as a result.”

He campaigned for — and lauded — the Starmer government’s move to abolish a two-child benefit cap.

Any intervention by this ex-PM would be significant.

4) The wider rank and file

The strength of feeling among other key backbench MPs who rebelled over Starmer’s plans will be an important barometer of how Burnham’s own reforms take shape.

Marie Tidball — who has a congenital disability affecting all four of her limbs and strongly campaigned for changes to Starmer’s reforms behind the scenes — welcomed Milburn’s messaging that there “won’t be crude cuts to benefits.”

Rachael Maskell, another vocal rebel, also welcomed the report, though warned employers should not “discriminate against young people being able to secure a job, not least if they experience severe anxiety or mental health challenges.”

Mainstream — a soft left Labour faction of which Burnham was an early backer — said in a statement there is “much to welcome” in the review. However, the group’s interim council warned in its X post that the ambition “must not come at the expense of anyone already struggling to get by.”

5) The Starmerites 

Ministers who served under Starmer know just how hard welfare reform is — and their views on Burnham’s plans will grab attention.

Former Chancellor Rachel Reeves is yet to comment on Milburn’s costly suggestions, but was busy defending her own record by highlighting a new report showing reduced levels of child poverty after she scrapped the two-child benefit cap.

Liz Kendall — who was work and pensions secretary under Starmer —was keen to raise a lack of AI skills and experience that could affect NEETs.

On Monday, five EU countries — Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands — announced plans to start deportations to a center in Rwanda from next year.

On Tuesday, Vincent Waiswa Bagiire, permanent secretary to Uganda’s foreign affairs ministry, confirmed that his country was interested in hosting a return hub.

Bagiire said Uganda had a “discussion” with the Netherlands but “we haven’t got far.” He didn’t say which other countries Uganda had been speaking with but said the talks were not that advanced: “Let me say that the discussion is at a stage of a cup of coffee.”

In June, European diplomats said Uganda and Uzbekistan were being discussed as potential locations for EU migration centers. However, Uganda has three criteria that need to be met before it can host a hub, Bagiire said on the sidelines of a conference in Vienna hosted by the International Centre for Migration Policy Development.

“If we are to establish a hub, it will be strictly for people of African origin; they should not have a criminal record; [and] no unaccompanied minors,” he said.

He added that the discussions involve “no more than 50” people, who would be sent to open facilities. “No detention, they’re not prisons — at all. People can integrate within the communities … they’re free to do whatever they need to do. The same way we treat our refugees,” he said.

]]> en Brussels signals unwillingness to be Burnham’s EU sounding board https://www.politico.eu/article/brussels-andy-burnham-eu-options-brexit-reset/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Tue, 17 Nov 2026 17:05:05 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9341457 LONDON — Andy Burnham wants to sound out options with the EU in his quest to ease Brexit. But Brussels is signaling that the U.K. prime minister needs to get his own plan together first.

The PM used a major foreign affairs speech Monday night to slow the timeline of his ambitions for bringing Britain closer to the bloc.

Instead of setting out “different options” for future relations around the time of Friday’s upcoming EU-U.K. summit, as he promised in September, he now wants to first fish for options with European allies.

But that timeline isn’t being welcomed with open arms in Brussels.

A senior EU diplomat with knowledge of the European Commission’s desired process made clear to POLITICO that the first step is for Britain to decide what changes it is considering.

“On the next steps, it should be about the U.K. first assessing its options and then engaging with the EU, rather than the other way around,” said the official, granted anonymity to discuss internal thinking.

Britain’s PM may, however, find more sympathetic ears among member states than in the European Commission.

A second EU diplomat said Burnham’s suggestion that he would sound out Brussels about different options “makes sense,” adding there is a “need to be pragmatic.” 

“There are very real mutual benefits to be unlocked,” they said. “Rather than getting lost in abstract debates about the ultimate destination, perhaps the more useful question is where we can make co-operation work better, here and now?”

A third EU diplomat said there could be a “gray area” in which both things are true.

While Britain can’t do “substantial negotiations” with the EU until there’s a “consensus” in the U.K., the same diplomat said it would be right for “some level of conversation with Brussels to see what’s sensible” so that realistic options can then be discussed with the British public.

But others agreed that the U.K. must provide sharper definition. A fourth EU diplomat said: “I think the next step in this process is that the EU needs a little more clarity on where the U.K. stands.”

A fifth said Burnham must first “include in his vision something that is realistic” which can then “be worked on together with the EU.”

Anand Menon, the director of the UK in a Changing Europe think tank, said a timeline where Brussels wants firmer proposals first should come as no surprise to Britain.

“The EU wants Britain to come to them and say this is the kind of relationship they want,” he said. “They want us to do that with a relationship that’s on offer rather than make up something that they are not willing to give.” 

Two U.K. government officials suggested that Burnham will still address future relations with Europe after the summit — but that this would be more limited to the “next steps” for the process. 

Later on Tuesday, Burnham seemed to soften his language again, telling Sky News he will consider “whether there are options” to deepen Britain’s relationship with the EU.  He said he would set them out alongside a government-wide 10-year plan due later this year. 

That would appear to fall short of what Burnham billed back in September, when addressing supporters in his first Labour Party conference speech as leader.

Back then, the U.K. prime minister promised “to lay out to the country what I believe the different options are for Britain’s long-term relationship with our European partners” at some point “around the summit” in Brussels on Friday.

He left a full-blown push to rejoin the EU open as one of the possibilities.

Since then, however, there has been a wave of hesitancy coming from within Burnham’s own Cabinet about the ramifications of reopening the fraught Brexit debate.

British public opinion may have changed greatly since the 2016 referendum, but U.K. politics remains scarred by the rancorous debates it produced.

Burnham used a Lord Mayor’s banquet speech in London on Monday evening to try cool off the timeline of his new approach.

“After the summit, we will initiate a discussion with our EU partners about options for our long-term relationship, recognizing that both Britain and the EU are very different to what they were,” he said.

“This will take time and we will present those options and our assessment of them to inform decisions in the next parliament. At every stage, the British people will be the boss.”

Andrew McDonald contributed reporting.

“It doesn’t add up,” said Retailleau.

“Instead of repairing the pensions system, they want to make the French pay,” she said.

The Wrocław regional prosecutor’s office said it had sent an indictment to the court in the southwestern town of Oleśnica, accusing Braun of depriving the doctor of her liberty, violating her bodily integrity and insulting her. The charges carry a maximum sentence of five years in prison, prosecutors added.

Braun and several supporters entered the Oleśnica hospital in April 2025 to confront a gynecologist who had carried out a late-term abortion on a patient whose life was at risk. The doctor said Braun held her for more than an hour by blocking the exit with his body.

Authorities charged six other people over the hospital incident. The indictment also covers property damage in the city of Opole and online calls by Braun in December 2023 to incite religious hatred and disrupt religious ceremonies.

The European Parliament lifted Braun’s immunity in the case in November 2025. Lawmakers have voted several times to strip him of legal protection, including over his use of a fire extinguisher to put out Hanukkah candles in the Polish parliament in 2023. He also faces separate charges of Holocaust denial.

Braun, who leads the ultranationalist Confederation of the Polish Crown party, came fourth in Poland’s 2025 presidential election.

Zelenskyy described the bridge strike as a response to Russian attacks against Ukrainian bridges that began a month ago.

 “We have repeatedly offered Russia steps toward de-escalation — and every proposal has been met with loud rejection. Russia strikes our infrastructure every day, including bridges in Zaporizhzhia, Dnipro, Kyiv, and the Odesa region. We are restoring our infrastructure. But we are also reminding Russia that war will always return to where it began,” Zelenskyy said in a statement.

The Russia-installed governor of Crimea, Sergei Aksenov, confirmed the strike, saying the bridge was closed until further notice, but provided no details of the damage.

Russia launched a bombing campaign against Ukrainian bridges on Oct. 1, choking logistics and causing huge public transport problems. The Russian defense ministry reported hitting Kyiv’s North and South bridges across the Dnipro River, linking the two sides of the Ukrainian capital.

Ukraine said its attack against the $3.7 billion Kerch Bridge is part of its response to the Russian campaign. The road and rail bridge is a key supply line for the 2.5 million people living on the Crimean Peninsula, illegally annexed by Russia in 2014, as well as for Russian forces stationed there.

The road portion has collapsed, and the extent of damage to the parallel rail bridge is uncertain, although the Russian transport ministry said Tuesday that limited traffic will resume on a single railway track. Without the bridge, Russia will have to rely on ferries and overland transport through occupied Ukraine — both routes subject to attack by Kyiv.

“Partial destruction of the bridge affects logistics, supply chains, and the morale and psychological state of the families of Russian military personnel, intelligence officers, and officials,” said Andrii Klymenko, head of the Black Sea and Baltic Strategic Research Monitoring Group.

Zelenskyy said the operation was carefully planned and gave a long list of the missiles and drones used.

“Our warriors gradually destroyed air defense systems, radars, electronic warfare equipment, and other designated targets on the way to the final objective. For this, they used Dovbush, Vendetta, Da Vinci, Sichen, Mich-2000, Ruta, Palianytsia, An-197, FP-1, FP-5 Flamingo, and R-360 Neptune,” the president said.

For the final stage, the Ukrainian army used Palianytsia drones to strike a road section of the bridge, while Neptune missiles, Ruta cruise missiles and FP-5 Flamingo heavy missiles struck the railway section.

“Using Flamingo, our warriors carried out a precision-guided strike — and the communications uplink worked flawlessly until the very last seconds,” Zelenskyy said, thanking Ukrainian weapons manufacturers.

Dutch-Ukrainian defense startup Destinus Group said that its Ruta missiles were used over two consecutive days. “Today, seven RUTA missiles hit the bridge, causing one span to collapse.”

“For years, the Russians convinced the entire world that the Crimean Bridge was one of the most heavily protected structures on the planet. Today, parts of it lie on the seabed,” said the press service of Ukraine’s SBU security agency.

Russian pro-war bloggers confirmed the scale of the attack.

“More than 10 Flamingo cruise missiles hit the target, plus a large number of drones. Given Russia’s air defense problems, the bridge could be ‘crushed’ by sheer numbers, without needing to overpower the defenses,” said the Rybar and Dva Mayora channels.

Russian officials downplayed the attack, with Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov saying the bridge would be rebuilt even better than it was before.

Russia-installed Sevastopol Governor Mikhail Razvozhaev said: “Supplies of food, fuel, diesel and other necessary goods continue. The bridge was not used for the delivery of goods that much, so the incident did not affect the supply of the city. Deliveries continue as usual.”

He said the bridge is largely used by private cars and buses. “Now the main task is to work out alternative logistical solutions for people who need to return home or continue their journey,” Razvozhaev said, asking people not to travel to Crimea until the authorities announce alternative routes.

Since Oct. 10, Ukrainian forces have targeted six other bridges near Crimea, creating growing problems for Russian logistics.

“The problem of destabilizing the rear in Crimea — and the entire southern grouping of forces— will only intensify if the railway section of the bridge is destroyed or significantly damaged, as this route is the most efficient one,” said Klymenko.

Disabling the bridge could make it more difficult for Russian forces to attack Odesa, Kherson and other regions along the Black Sea, said Ukrainian navy spokesperson Dmytro Pletenchuk.

“With the bridge damaged and land routes to Crimea under Ukrainian operational control, it would now be significantly harder to deliver those drones Russia sends to Ukraine from the peninsula,” he said.

]]> en Rwanda hits back at asylum-seeker return hub criticism https://www.politico.eu/article/rwanda-hit-back-return-hub-criticism/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Tue, 17 Nov 2026 13:50:47 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=article&p=9339543 VIENNA — Rwanda’s interior minister has rebuked criticism of a plan by five European Union countries to deport failed asylum-seekers to his country.

Austria, Denmark, Germany, Greece and the Netherlands on Monday announced a partnership with Rwanda to set up a deportation hub. They aim to send the first asylum-seekers to the African country in 2027.

The plan comes after the EU adopted legislation that allows countries to negotiate deals to build such “return hubs” outside the bloc — as long as they meet human rights standards. The announcement led to a storm of protest from civil society and human rights groups, which said the fundamental rights of people sent to Rwanda cannot be guaranteed.

Rwanda’s interior minister, Vincent Biruta, disagreed.

“Human rights in Rwanda are respected and granted to everyone and specifically to refugees who choose to come to our country,” Biruta said Tuesday, speaking on a panel at a conference in Vienna hosted by the International Centre for Migration Policy Development.

He argued his country’s migration policies are among the “most progressive” as they allow refugees to work and start a business.

In a joint warning against the plan Monday, 47 organizations pointed to a 2023 court decision that slapped down the United Kingdom’s plans to process asylum seekers’ claims in Rwanda. It cited “substantial grounds” to believe that people sent to the African nation would be exposed “to a real risk of ill-treatment by reason of refoulement” — referring to a practice whereby people are forcibly moved to countries where they face real threats. Under a 2013 deal with Israel, people sent to Rwanda “were routinely moved clandestinely to Uganda,” the court added.

Biruta said he was “not surprised” by NGOs’ warnings and said the government faced “the same issue” when it was making plans with the U.K. Those plans “didn’t work but … helped to improve our asylum system,” he added.

NGOs “always … say that nothing is working, that our human rights record is bad,” Biruta said, “but I’d like them to come forward with an alternative solution.” 

EU ministers repeatedly stressed Monday that their partnership with Rwanda would meet international and European standards. Biruta said his country would put in place an independent monitoring mechanism and that it wants to involve the International Organization for Migration and the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees.

Details about such mechanisms and cooperation, as well as how the EU countries and Rwanda will divide responsibilities for the refugees’ wellbeing, have not yet been revealed.

“There are still some technical things that have to be solved, including where [the responsibility of ] Europe ends and where Rwanda starts,” Danish Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen told POLITICO after the plan’s announcement.

Human rights groups don’t believe the countries can come up with a framework that will guarantee migrants’ rights are respected.

Rwanda has an abysmal human rights record, is responsible for serious abuses and war crimes in eastern Congo and engages in transnational repression, Judith Sunderland, senior associate director in the refugee and migrant rights division of Human Rights Watch, told POLITICO.

“No amount of nominal safeguards will be sufficient to mitigate the risks of serious human rights violations, particularly as there is unlikely to be any way to implement effective monitoring or seek accountability,” she said. “Given its track record, the fact that Rwanda was even considered, much less chosen, justifies deep skepticism about EU rhetoric about respecting people’s rights.”

Nektaria Stamouli contributed reporting.

]]> en EU countries postpone vote to lift Brazilian chicken ban https://www.politico.eu/article/eu-countries-postpone-vote-to-lift-brazilian-chicken-ban/?utm_source=RSS_Feed&utm_medium=RSS&utm_campaign=RSS_Syndication Tue, 17 Nov 2026 12:27:43 +0000 https://www.politico.eu/?post_type=pro&p=9339045 BRUSSELS — Brazilian poultry meat won’t return to European supermarket shelves for now, after EU countries on Tuesday put off a vote that would have lifted a ban that has been in place since September.

A committee with representatives of the EU’s member countries had been set to vote on the decision, but this was canceled as they failed to reach an agreement, European Commission spokesperson Eva Hrncirova said.

The Commission said it would address the issue with the aim to discuss it again Dec. 7-8 at the next meeting of the Standing Committee on Plants, Animals, Food and Feed (PAFF).

Brazil failed to prove it complies with EU rules on antimicrobials and the EU halted poultry imports on Sept. 3. A subsequent Commission audit at the end of that month found that Brazil’s controls again meet the necessary requirements.

Still, a number of countries “requested further clarifications on the system put in place by Brazil,” Hrncirova said.

Tuesday’s vote was postponed after it became clear that enough member countries were likely to oppose the agreement to form a blocking minority, according to three EU diplomats familiar with the matter.

The poultry dispute has added to tensions over the EU’s trade deal with the South American Mercosur bloc, which includes Brazil and took effect in May. Farmers in countries including France and Poland have opposed the agreement, warning that cheaper South American imports would expose them to unfair competition.

Bartosz Brzeziński and Camille Gijs contributed reporting.

EUobserver https://euobserver.com Independent EU journalism Tue, 17 Nov 2026 18:05:17 +0000 en-US hourly 1 https://wordpress.org/?v=7.1.4 UK sanctions on Israel leave EU unmoved, despite ‘man-made catastrophe’ in Gaza https://euobserver.com/249585/uk-sanctions-on-israel-leave-eu-unmoved-despite-man-made-catastrophe-in-gaza/ Tue, 17 Nov 2026 17:58:31 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=249585 In a voice from Gaza, Ahmed Abu Jami, a 28-year-old doctor, who lives in Khan Younis, told EUobserver via WhatsApp: "Things are bad, really Gaza is descending into hell."]]> New UK sanctions against Israel have spotlighted the EU’s inaction on the “man-made catastrophe” in Gaza and raging aggression in the West Bank.

The UK blacklisted eight Israeli construction firms which build homes for West Bank settlers on Tuesday (17 November), as well as the Tzav 9 activist group, which blocks humanitarian aid to Gaza.

“My message on ‌E1 is clear: do not bid, do not build,” said British foreign secretary Ed Miliband, referring to the new ‘E1’ settlement designed to cut the West Bank in half and kill off the prospect of a two-state solution.

Israel is currently being led by a caretaker government amid post-election coalition talks.

Miliband noted that “more settlements have been approved under the four years of this Israeli government [of prime minister Benjamin Netanyahu] than in the previous 20 years.”

Floods in Gaza, after Israel destroyed its EU-funded water-management infrastructure, have left 4,000 people homeless, while 1.4 million people are living in tents in wintry weather, but Israel was blocking deliveries of tarpaulins and timber, Miliband added.

EU foreign minsters are also clear-eyed about what Israel is doing in Gaza and the West Bank.

]]> EU asylum agency floats idea of foreign ‘processing centres’ to handle asylum claims https://euobserver.com/249553/eu-asylum-agency-floats-idea-of-foreign-processing-centres-to-handle-asylum-claims/ Tue, 17 Nov 2026 16:57:07 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=249553 Innovative solutions is a catch all phrase that describes return hubs in Rwanda and Italy's controversial deal with Albania. Now it also applies to "process centres" for asylum seeker hopefuls.]]> Late last year, the EU tweaked laws allowing member states to have a person’s claim for asylum heard somewhere abroad.

Now, discussions are taking place to create a so-called “processing centre” in a foreign country, where the asylum seekers who initially landed in Europe would have their case for protection heard.

Nina Gregori, who heads the Malta-based European Union Agency for Asylum (EUAA), floated the idea in a passing remark about possible innovative solutions on migration control at the International Centre for Migration Policy Development (ICMPD) conference in Vienna on Tuesday (17 November).

‘Innovative solutions’ is a catch-all phrase that has also applied to return hubs in Rwanda and Italy’s controversial deal with Albania.

Read more

Five EU countries tout Rwanda deportation partnership, but no formal deal as key details remain secret

Asked to further elaborate, she told EUobserver that the idea is already backed by European law, citing the so-called “safe-third country concept”.

The concept essentially shifts EU member states’ responsibility for processing asylum claims to foreign states, even if the asylum seeker has never set foot in the country. The concept itself is not new.

]]> France dethrones Sweden as EU gender equality leader — but overall progress is slowing https://euobserver.com/249501/france-dethrones-sweden-as-eu-gender-equality-leader-but-overall-progress-is-slowing/ Tue, 17 Nov 2026 16:12:20 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=249501 Europe still has a significant gender gap. It's in employment, in who takes care of children, in places of power. It's stronger in places like Cyprus and Bulgaria, while Spain and Denmark prioritised its gender politics. But full gender equality is still a distant goal, as Europe still lags behind pre-pandemic levels of parity. ]]> France is leading the way on gender equality in the EU, according to a study published on Tuesday (17 November), with more female representation at decision-making levels becoming the main push for gender equality. 

The European institute for gender equality (EIGE) publishes an annual index measuring how close the EU is to equality between men and women. This year’s report shows a small improvement, though noting European societies are yet to recover from a post-pandemic slump in progress. The agency says this is “a sign that the momentum built over the past decade is losing strength”.

The proportion of women in positions of power has grown faster than in any other sector, with increased representation in economic and social decision-making positions across several member states. Even so, it is still the lowest-scoring area of the index.

While still remaining severely underrepresented in leadership positions, particularly compared to the Nordic countries, France and Spain have encouraged more policy action on gender equality.

Read more

EU reduces funds for women’s rights groups, in wider budget bonfire of good causes

However, some of the Nordic nations have started to fall back. 

Sweden, whose 13-year record in leading the gender equality struggle was overtaken this year by France, is “kind of stagnating,” EIGE’s statistics officer, Davide Barbieri, told EUobserver.

“We are going in a good direction, but we can do even better, and we need to do that together, member states as well, its regions, civil societies, companies, employers,” said EU commission executive vice-president for social rights, Roxana Mînzatu, at Tuesday’s launch event for the index in Brussels.

“How we make sure that gender equality contributes and fuels growth, it’s always three levels that we need to act upon: it’s skills and education, it’s the quality of jobs, and it’s the availability of care”

]]> EU freezes €62.5m of Slovakia’s recovery funds over plans linked to ousted environment minister https://euobserver.com/249456/eu-freezes-e62-5m-of-slovakias-recovery-funds-over-plans-linked-to-ousted-environment-minister/ Tue, 17 Nov 2026 14:55:16 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=249456 Internal government warnings, downgraded wind plans and controversial zoning tweaks by ousted environment minister Taraba’s team now emerge at the heart of the Commission’s decision, exposing how months of behind-the-scenes manoeuvring may have sabotaged Slovakia’s own green transition money. ]]> The European Commission has suspended €62.5m from Slovakia’s eighth recovery-plan payment over inadequacies in the zoning of national parks and preparation of a wind energy zone.

The sum concerns the Recovery and Resilience Facility, part of the EU’s plan to emerge stronger from the Covid-19 pandemic by issuing funds for the green transition and country-specific investments.

After the commission’s decision on Monday (16 November), the Slovak government now has two months to prepare its position and send the missing documentation to Brussels.

The commission confirmed it only partially approved the eighth recovery-plan payment worth €735m, adding that Slovakia had not fulfilled two commitments concerning national park zoning and preparation of a wind farm zone.

In its plans, Slovakia had not classified all threatened forests under the highest level of protection available. And the country also failed to show that the area chosen for a wind energy acceleration zone was suitable for building wind farms with a capacity of at least 300 megawatts.

As a result, €62.5m is expected to be withheld.

“Should the Commission, following Slovakia’s observations, confirm its assessment that the milestones in question have not been satisfactorily fulfilled, it will proportionally reduce the amount corresponding to this milestone and target, out of the total €548m under this payment request,” read an EU press release.

Read more

MEPs warn against EU rush to restarting funds for Hungary while corruption and plurality concerns remain

Ex-environment minister to blame?

Both problematic milestones are linked to steps taken by the former Slovak environment minister Tomáš Taraba.

Taraba was removed from office in September 2026 after falling out with the right-wing Slovak National Party who had appointed him in 2023.

Slovak prime minister Robert Fico has taken over his office for the time being.

The office of the deputy prime minister, temporarily headed by education minister Tomáš Drucker (belonging to the left-wing Voice party), blames the previous cabinet for forest and wind energy zoning plan problems.

]]> EU Commission again rebukes Temu over failure to stop illegal product sales, exposing Chinese giant to another hefty fine https://euobserver.com/249412/eu-commission-again-rebukes-temu-over-failure-to-stop-illegal-product-sales-risking-another-hefty-fine/ Tue, 17 Nov 2026 11:29:31 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=249412 Temu failed to take sufficient action to stop illegal or unsafe products being put on sale, the EU Commission has found preliminarily. It comes as part of a probe into the company's compliance with the Digital Services Act. The Chinese shopping website has disputed the latest findings.]]> Temu failed to take sufficient action to stop illegal or unsafe products being put on sale, the EU Commission concluded on Tuesday (17 November), as part of a lengthy probe to assess its compliance with EU law launched in 2024.

The commission found that the online marketplace had “ineffective controls” in place to ensure that products sold on its platform met EU safety requirements.

It also says this amounts to a breach of the Digital Services Act, the EU’s rulebook for online platforms, which has been in force since August 2023.

The commission’s latest findings of insufficient mitigation against the sale of illegal items follow a decision in May that Temu’s risk assessments were inadequate, leading Temu to pay a €200m fine.

The Chinese online shopping retailer has been investigated over the alleged listing of illegal products, as well as addictive design, recommendation algorithms and data-sharing.

Temu has more than 120 million users in the EU, according to commission officials.

“We’re happy to see the Commission has taken consumer organisations complaints and evidence seriously regarding how Temu’s fails to meet its obligations. Consumers should be able to shop safely on these very large online marketplaces,” said Agustín Reyna, director general of consumer protection body BEUC.

Read more

]]> [Interview] Czech MEP Niedermayer slams Babiš opposition to new EU budget revenue: ‘It’s short-sighted’ https://euobserver.com/249160/interview-czech-mep-niedermayer-slams-babis-opposition-to-new-eu-budget-revenue-its-short-sighted/ Tue, 17 Nov 2026 09:59:47 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=249160 From missed IT revolutions to costly nuclear bets, EU Parliament's economic policy vice-chair Luděk Niedermayer sketches a stark choice for European capitals: keep blaming Brussels for their woes, clinging to national budgets, or allow the EU to levy its own targeted taxes on negative externalities to better compete with the US and China.]]> The EU should introduce its own taxes to discourage the consumption of harmful products such as tobacco and strengthen its ability to compete with the US and China, Czech MEP Luděk Niedermayer said in an interview. A member of the centre-right European People’s Party (EPP), Niedermayer is a former vice-governor of the Czech central bank and vice-chair of the European Parliament’s committee on economic and monetary affairs.

The 2024 report of former Italian prime minister Mario Draghi delivered an unflattering assessment of the EU’s competitiveness. Do you fear that divisions between national capitals in the EU means the union will have to rely on enhanced cooperation more often?

Luděk Niedermayer: I would not describe enhanced cooperation as something to fear — in many cases, it is a useful solution when all countries simply do not agree on something that would in fact move the EU forward.

As an MEP, I worked on a mechanism to promote equity financing for companies instead of loans. In my view, that mechanism is very good and has clear economic justification. It stalled in the Council, blocked by the unanimity requirement for tax matters.

“National leaders declare their support for Draghi’s findings, but do precisely the opposite in negotiations on the European budget.”

But if, through enhanced cooperation, a workable concept could be created for a group of countries without undermining the single market, it would clearly add value.

The same applies to the so-called 28th legal regime [EU Inc]. If someone offered me a choice between a weak compromise and a strong regime for half of the EU’s member states, I would choose the latter.

The red line is fragmentation of the single market itself, for instance by protectionist barriers between member states. It cannot be that someone says: ‘I am in the single market, but I do not import apples from Poland,’ or, ‘I am in the single market, but I will not import cars from Czechia and Slovakia.’

That would be the end of the road, but nobody is considering that.

So what follows from this?

The Draghi report focuses on key European sectors for economic growth. Many member states blame their economic failures on EU regulations, while other countries operating within the same legislative framework achieve excellent results, prosper and reduce their debt.

National leaders declare their support for Draghi’s findings, but do precisely the opposite in negotiations on the European budget. [Another former Italian prime minister] Enrico Letta’s report on the single market is equally crucial. It outlines changes that could be implemented more quickly.

You are working on the 28th regime with former Slovak prime minister and current Renew MEP Ľudovít Ódor with the aim to enable companies to grow without having to hire dozens of tax advisers in each EU country. Given that taxation falls within national competence, is it realistic to establish a workable model?

I consider the EU Commission’s initial proposal to simplify the establishment of companies across borders good. Digitalisation, simplification and acceleration are a good direction to take as a starting point.

Read more

EU unveils ’28th regime’, creating bloc-wide business code

I do not think it is essential for the 28th regime to be used by tens of thousands of companies across the EU; it would be most effective for start-ups and expanding companies, for which the costs of extending across Europe are greatest. Limiting this regime to a specific type of company in exchange for its high effectiveness is an acceptable compromise.

Looking at the wider business environment, 60 of the world’s 100 largest companies are from the US and fewer than 20 are European. And Chiness giants are growing faster than us. Why is Europe unable to produce global giants like Google or Anthropic?

One reason we are absent from these rankings is that rapid growth needed took place in the IT sector, where Europe simply fell asleep. Parts of our economy and politics remained stuck in the analogue era, and we did not realise how important this was.

“Rapid growth needed took place in the IT sector, where Europe simply fell asleep.”

And when high-quality IT know-how emerged in Europe, it moved to the US at a certain stage of growth. I see three reasons for this.

What are those three reasons?

First, the US has an incomparably larger financing market than the EU.

Second, other legal environments are more certain. The US state Delaware has created the world’s best commercial legal system, under which most large US companies are incorporated. Not because of taxes, but because of legal certainty. Delaware has a commercial law system that no one can match.

Read more

MEPs back new EU‑wide ‘28th regime’ businesses plan — but fear a ‘European Delaware’

Third, non-EU markets have higher demands for new players. The US market is far more willing to buy products from young start-ups, while Europe prefers established suppliers.

But I will add a caveat: a larger company does not mean a better company. Our weakness in the IT sector has cost us economic growth and created a dangerous technological dependency.

The Draghi report warns of Europe’s strategic vulnerabilities in raw materials, chips and security. How should the EU respond to Chinese dominance in these fields?

China has made good decisions and backed them with massive state aid for industrial sectors. This would not be possible in Europe.

China also disregards ethical and environmental standards in extracting raw materials. But its technologies are of high quality.

There are areas in which we can benefit from the fact that China has invested heavily and produces an excess supply of quality goods.

Solar panels are one example. Cheap solar panels are helping us move towards achieving our climate goals.

In critical sectors, we must use a combination of supportive and protective measures to build our own capacity or diversify suppliers.

Where there are unfair state subsidies, we must impose duties to offset them, but not blanket protectionism, the cost of which consumers would bear in the form of higher prices for goods.

Read more

One supply scare pushed China into renewables. Two real crises still haven’t woken Europe up

Chinese technology is also a threat…

In terms of security, we must ask ourselves the extent to which there is a risk that China will use technology as a weapon, like [Russian president] Vladimir Putin does with gas.

We must be careful not to use security arguments as a pretext for closing the market. We would deprive ourselves of competition that could bring down the prices of goods. If we neglect this, it also becomes a security risk.

Is the growth of China’s electric-vehicle sector a threat to the automotive industry in Eastern Europe?

I have the impression that this concern stems from the situation a few years ago. Dependence on batteries has gradually decreased thanks to dozens of new investments and research projects in the EU, although it remains significant. In 10 to 20 years, recycling will play a key role, reducing dependence on raw materials.

European carmakers made a huge strategic mistake by suppressing the development of electric vehicles and promoting combustion engines.

]]> Listen: What do France’s centre-right candidates want for Europe? https://euobserver.com/249396/listen-what-do-frances-centre-right-candidates-want-for-europe/ Tue, 17 Nov 2026 09:04:25 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=249396 In the race for the French presidential election, there are already four names on the centre-right: Gabriel Attal, Bruno Retailleau, David Lisnard and Édouard Philippe. For now, they haven't reached an agreement to join forces and put forward a single candidate.]]>

Production: By Europod, in co-production with Sphera Network.

EUobserver is proud to have an editorial partnership with Europod to co-publish the podcast series “Briefed” hosted by Léa Marchal. The podcast is available on all major platforms.

Find the full transcript below: 

In the race for the French presidential election, there are already four names on the centre-right: Gabriel Attal, Bruno Retailleau, David Lisnard and Édouard Philippe. For now, they haven’t reached an agreement to join forces and put forward a single candidate.

But do they share the same vision of Europe? None of these candidates question France’s membership of the European Union, or the fundamental rules governing it. Nor do they call for changes to the EU treaties, unlike some other candidates.

The differences are more about how critical they are of the EU’s current functioning. For example, both David Lisnard and Bruno Retailleau believe the European Commission sometimes goes beyond its original remit.

Retailleau wants to make it possible to bring cases before the Court of Justice of the European Union when the commission is accused of overstepping its powers.

Lisnard, meanwhile, wants to strengthen the role of the Council and the European Parliament, which he considers more legitimate institutions.

Read more

What Marine Le Pen and Alice Weidel are planning for Brussels

He also takes a particularly strong stance on national sovereignty. He opposes situations in which EU law prevents member states from taking certain decisions. When that happens, he believes the question should be put to the people through a referendum.

As for the biggest issue of the moment, the EU’s multiannual budget, none of the four candidates has set out a clear position on the size of the EU budget, or on how much France should contribute to it.

This is quite different from Marine Le Pen’s pledge to halve France’s contribution to the EU budget. You won’t find anything of the sort in the centre-right candidates’ programmes.

Édouard Philippe puts considerable emphasis on mobilising private investment to finance innovation. That’s a position often associated with the more fiscally conservative EU member states: rather than injecting more public money into the economy, they want to make better use of private savings.

Gabriel Attal takes a somewhat different approach. For example, he proposes a common European artificial intelligence policy, backed by its own dedicated budget, much like the Common Agricultural Policy.

Read more

Europe’s youth take to the streets as the post‑war promise of a better life breaks down

And he explicitly suggests that this could be financed through common European borrowing.

Speaking of the Common Agricultural Policy, do they agree on what should happen to EU farming subsidies? Very much so. All four candidates place considerable importance on the CAP and want to protect France’s share of the funding.

That’s hardly surprising: France is one of the biggest beneficiaries of the Common Agricultural Policy, which provides substantial financial support to French farmers.

When it comes to agriculture, there’s one proposal from Bruno Retailleau that stands out: he doesn’t want Ukraine to join the EU’s agricultural market.

This isn’t particularly surprising, actually. Many Europeans share this view, especially in countries where agriculture plays a major role. But unlike Retailleau, the other centre-right candidates don’t openly state this position.

And what about Ukraine more broadly? Do they have clear positions on the war and European support? All in all, yes, although they don’t go into much detail. Their programmes are almost silent on this issue.

Read more

Europe’s centre parties are collapsing – and, for the first time, the far-right are collaborating, rather than fighting

However, their public statements are clear: all four have consistently supported Ukraine, including through weapons deliveries and the possible use of frozen Russian assets to finance the country’s reconstruction.

They also agree on the need to strengthen Europe’s defence capabilities.

One way to do this, they argue, is to give preference to European-made military equipment. In other words, European countries should prioritise buying weapons and defence systems from European manufacturers rather than relying on American suppliers.

Gabriel Attal talks about this extensively, and Édouard Philippe also explicitly supports the idea. Attal goes a step further, proposing an investment fund specifically designed to support small and medium-sized businesses in the defence sector.

So, while the four candidates don’t have identical programmes, their overall vision of Europe is relatively similar. The main differences lie in how they want to reform the EU institutions, finance common priorities and protect national sovereignty.

]]> Only Stockholm, Helsinki and Copenhagen meet EU air pollution rules, as stricter enforcement looms https://euobserver.com/249193/eus-stricter-airpollution-law-looms-but-nearly-all-major-cities-are-still-offtrack/ Tue, 17 Nov 2026 05:30:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=249193 Apart from Copenhagen, Stockholm and Helsinki, no other major European city currently meets the revised EU limits for nitrogen dioxide and particulate matter - exposure to which caused a combined 216,000 excess deaths in 2023 alone. ]]> Only three cities are on track to reach EU pollution goals by the end of the year, a new study revealed on Tuesday (17 November), enforcing existing divisions between northern and south-eastern European cities. 

Copenhagen, Greater Stockholm and Greater Helsinki were the only major European cities or conurbations to have met new EU limits for pollution, while the vast majority of European cities are falling short of the new standards – expected to be transposed into member state law by December 2026.

Despite progress noted across bustling cities such as Paris, Stuttgart, and Oslo, the Clean Cities report found no other major European city to currently meet the revised EU limits for nitrogen dioxide and particulate matter, exposure to which caused a combined 216,000 excess deaths in 2023 alone. 

Clean Cities, a coalition of 150 NGOs and grassroots groups, found reductions in pollutants to mostly in cities that had implemented clean transport measures such as low-emission zones and electric buses, as well as changes in residential heating, improved cycling routes and school streets. 

Read more

‘Made in Europe’ and low-carbon rules up for debate as EU eyes industrial law deal 

“The strong air quality performance of the Helsinki metropolitan area is above all the result of decades of consistent, long-term efforts,” said Antti Wemberg, senior specialist at the Finnish ministry of environment.

“The city of Helsinki has been proactive in communicating air quality issues and providing practical guidance on how individuals can improve air quality through their own everyday decisions and activities,” Wemberg told EUobserver. 

The European Environment agency found that 9 out of 10 Europeans are still exposed to air pollution at concentrations unsafe for human health, and this is largely concentrated in areas in south, east and central Europe. 

Tuesday’s study found the most polluted urban centres to be in Zagreb, Bucharest, and worst-of-all, Athens.

]]> ‘Forever chemicals’ lobbyists met EU Commission 37 times in push to escape ban ahead of key decision https://euobserver.com/249008/forever-plastics-lobbyists-met-eu-commission-37-times-in-bid-to-escape-ban/ Tue, 17 Nov 2026 05:01:00 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=249008 As the European Chemicals Agency finalises its conclusions on so-called 'forever chemicals', a new report reveals regular contact between senior European Commission officials and industry lobbyists.]]> The EU’s attempt to restrict so-called “forever chemicals” (PFAS) is facing a coordinated industry push for exemptions that could leave the ban badly weakened, a report revealed on Tuesday (17 November).

The findings by the watchdog Corporate Europe Observatory (CEO) come as the European Chemicals Agency (ECHA) prepares its final assessment of the proposed ban, the last scientific step before the dossier lands on the European Commission’s desk for a decision.

The commission has signalled that it favours banning PFAS (per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances) in some consumer products but may take a softer line on industrial uses, which it sees as vital to Europe’s competitiveness in sectors such as semiconductors, batteries and clean-tech manufacturing.

With different parts of the industry each lobbying for their own exemptions or longer transition periods, campaigners fear the result could be a restriction full of loopholes.

The fluoropolymer lobby, made up by companies and groups including Chemours, Daikin, Arkema and the trade association Plastics Europe, want fluoropolymers fully exempted from the PFAS ban. They say that they are essential to Europe’s green and digital transitions and that no viable alternatives exist.

Since Ursula von der Leyen’s second term as commission president began, they have met the commission at least 37 times to discuss PFAS. That amounts to at least one meeting every third week, almost entirely with the most senior officials.

But due to incomplete meeting records and vague descriptions of some meetings, the figure is likely to be higher, warned CEO.

    ]]>         What Marine Le Pen and Alice Weidel are planning for Brussels https://euobserver.com/248722/what-marine-le-pen-and-alice-weidel-are-planning-for-brussels/ Mon, 16 Nov 2026 14:52:23 +0000 https://euobserver.com/?p=248722 The AfD's Alice Weidel envisages reducing EU powers under existing rules within three years, pursuing treaty reform within seven, and using Germany's budgetary leverage along the way. Hot on her heels, Marine Le Pen is looking towards national elections across Europe to build a coalition of like-minded governments.]]> It’s been an early Christmas for Europe’s centre-left, watching even the most unshakeable populists stumble. Viktor Orbán’s defeat in April sent shockwaves through Europe after 16 years of entrenched cronyism, while Serbia followed hot on the heels of this October, reminding leaders that clinging to power is not the same as keeping the vote.

    And just when the drama seemed to subside, American voters, fed up with soaring prices, showed that the fury that lifts politicians to power can just as swiftly sweep them away.

    Should Brussels’ centre-left pop the champagne? Not so fast. The trouble with celebrating populists’ downfall is that the grievances that put them in office are still simmering.

    Alice Weidel in Germany and Marine Le Pen in France, for one, seem to have read the room. 

    ‘Frexit’ and the single currency

    Putting reform before withdrawal is no small thing. Le Pen has already ditched Frexit, while Weidel’s AfD is reconsidering its longstanding hostility to the euro.

    These are not merely plans to trim ‘Brussels bureaucracy’; they strike at the question of who gets the final say in Europe.

    For Germany’s export-dependent economy, leaving Europe’s single market and common currency could carry an uncomfortable price tag (€690bn).

    Rather, Weidel has baked into her proposed major reform of Germany’s role in the EU a shift from, in her words, its current paymaster role to one which reinforces German sovereignty.

    Weidel has even put a timetable on the ambition.

    Her party’s roadmap envisages reducing EU powers under existing rules within three years, pursuing treaty reform within seven, and using Germany’s budgetary leverage along the way. Hot on her heels, Le Pen is looking towards national elections across Europe to build a coalition of like-minded governments. 

    Both appear to recognise that power in Brussels can begin with power at home.

    And with populist parties gaining influence across the continent, changing the EU from within may offer more political leverage than another Brexit season.  

    Who holds the purse strings?

    The timing of Le Pen and Weidel’s rise could hardly be more uncomfortable. As the EU hammers out its nearly €2 trillion 2028–2034 budget, it is juggling the costly business of backing Ukraine, beefing up defence, and answering demands to spend more at home.

    For Le Pen and Weidel, Brussels’ budgetary nightmare could be the ideal stage to show who should really control the purse strings.

    Enter Le Pen, stage right.

    If in power following the 2027 French elections, Le Pen wants to slash France’s EU contributions while simultaneously demanding the return of €2.2bn annually in customs duties collected at French borders.

    Yet France is also a major beneficiary of EU agricultural funding.

    Cutting Brussels’ contributions could therefore raise awkward questions about who picks up the bill for French farmers. A September 2026 German Council on Foreign Relations study warns that a future French government could exploit the national ratification process to obstruct the EU’s revenue arrangements, even after a painstaking budget agreement. 

    Even if Brussels manages to hammer out a deal before French voters have their say, the squabble over who foots the bill is unlikely to vanish.

    The EU’s revenue rules still demand a chorus of unanimous approval and a round of national rubber-stamping, which could hand a future French government a fresh bargaining chip long after the ink dries on any spending pact.

    Brussels still faces the headache of actually securing the cash, with nationalist parties like AfD threatening to, if in power, block decisions until their demands are met. 

    Crowded calendar for 2027

    And Brussels has already spotted the storm. Emmanuel Macron has urged EU leaders to reach a budget agreement before the year is out, warning that Europe’s crowded 2027 election calendar could make negotiations considerably harder.

    But rushing through a deal does not guarantee it will put the matter to bed.

    Even after governments agree on spending, a future French administration could still challenge the arrangements for financing it. And while Weidel’s AfD remains outside Germany’s government, its proposed roadmap offers a glimpse of how the country’s financial weight might be used to demand wider institutional changes.

    The warning for Brussels is clear: the next Eurosceptic challenge may not come from those threatening to storm out, but from those determined to stay and rewrite the rulebook.

      <title>Deutsche Bank dismissed warnings about dealings with risky clients, reports claim</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/17/deutsche-bank-dimissed-warnings-risky-clients-reports-claim</link>
      <description><p>International investigation using trove of leaked internal data allegedly shows German bank overlooked compliance concerns to safeguard profits</p><p>Deutsche Bank reportedly dismissed warnings about its dealings with risky clients, including high-profile Russian oligarchs, to protect profits, the findings of an investigation into a trove of leaked bank documents indicate.</p><p>A leak of 15m internal files is reported to show that the troubled German bank repeatedly ignored concerns by its compliance officers about its risk-taking, despite having already <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2019/apr/17/deutsche-bank-faces-action-over-20bn-russian-money-laundering-scheme">been caught being used to launder billions of dollars</a> for Russian criminals, spies and oligarchs between 2010 and 2015.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/2026/nov/17/deutsche-bank-dimissed-warnings-risky-clients-reports-claim">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>Markets drop ahead of Nvidia’s results; Jensen Huang says he’d be ‘honoured’ to return as CEO – as it happened</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/business/live/2026/nov/17/uk-jobs-market-wage-growth-payrolls-unemployment-milburn-china-us-chips-latest-news-updates</link>
      <description><p>Rolling coverage of the latest economic and financial news</p><ul><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/17/nvidia-jensen-huang-statement"><strong>Jensen Huang says he would be ‘honored’ to return to Nvidia as CEO</strong></a></p></li><li><p><a href="https://www.theguardian.com/global/2026/nov/16/jensen-huang-nvidia-ceo-china"><strong>Jensen Huang’s departure as Nvidia CEO becomes a political proxy war</strong></a></p></li></ul><p><strong>China has threatened to retaliate against the US after Washington tightened restrictions on remote access to AI chips and servers.</strong></p><p>At a press conference on Tuesday, China’s foreign ministry spokesperson <strong>Guo</strong> <strong>Jiakun</strong> said Beijing would take “necessary measures” to safeguard its own interests, saying:</p><p>“The US has repeatedly overstretched the concept of national security, abused export controls and even interfered in China’s normal trade and technological cooperation with other countries, unjustifiably suppressing the development of China’s high-tech industries.”</p><p>“This is the worst situation possible for China because the last thing they want to see is any new restrictions on their access to chips.”</p><p>“Export controls are what upset them practically more than anything else right now other than maybe Taiwan.”</p><p>Deutsche plotted an expansion of its <a href="https://www.ft.com/content/bf775dda-4148-49f9-a8b4-a4a02f44207e">notorious Russia business</a> under chief executive Christian Sewing, over-ruling the fears of its compliance team about the bank’s Kremlin-connected clientele as geopolitical storm clouds gathered.</p><p>The bank <a href="https://www.ft.com/content/784cbdc7-c852-4081-b1e5-390779e9fad1">accidentally leaked Trump’s tax statements</a> during his first presidential term and kept the mistake secret from the White House, with Sewing briefed on its handling of the crisis.</p><p>Deutsche processed almost $600mn of suspicious <a href="https://www.ft.com/content/72ac6fee-55f3-4db5-a1e3-873ef39c0b96">payments linked to Jeffrey Epstein</a>, a far higher figure than previously known.</p><p>A <a href="https://www.ft.com/content/4f8dae68-bfec-43bd-bef6-b830815ec538">catalogue</a> of compliance deficiencies, governance weaknesses, ineptitude and technology failings, including a confession to regulators that Deutsche was in effect “operating outside of law and order”.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/business/live/2026/nov/17/uk-jobs-market-wage-growth-payrolls-unemployment-milburn-china-us-chips-latest-news-updates">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/16/companies-trump-tariff-refunds-corporate-bonuses</link>
      <description><p>Some firms are directing refunds to corporate leadership instead of reimbursing consumers, ProPublica finds </p><p>Several companies that received refunds for paying <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/donaldtrump">Donald Trump</a>’s <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/trump-tariffs">tariffs</a> have put those funds towards corporate bonuses instead of reimbursing consumers, <a href="https://www.propublica.org/article/trump-tariff-refunds-corporate-bonuses">an investigation</a> from ProPublica has found.</p><p>After analyzing securities filings and earnings calls, ProPublica identified at least nine companies who said they are receiving tariff refunds and noted they are directing some of those funds to their leadership.</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/us-news/2026/nov/16/companies-trump-tariff-refunds-corporate-bonuses">Continue reading...</a></description>

      <title>Farewell to Elon Musk’s Cybertruck. Has any car ever been more repellent? | Arwa Mahdawi</title>
      <link>https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/nov/11/farewell-cybertruck-elon-musk-car-repellent</link>
      <description><p>Safety campaigners have condemned it and owners have complained about it. Goodbye to a steel monstrosity seemingly designed by a five-year-old</p><p>Elon Musk is having a rough go of it, isn’t he? The world’s richest man spent almost half a billion dollars on the <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/04/elon-musk-midterm-spending-analysis">midterms</a> in a failed attempt to defend Republican control of government. Now the tech mogul, who moved from California to Texas to escape Democrats and regulations, finds himself in a newly blue state. He also finds himself the subject of an unflattering <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/film/2026/sep/08/musk-review-epic-study-worlds-richest-most-banal-man-elon-film">documentary</a> and, if the Democrats follow through on threats to investigate him, could potentially be in a spot of legal bother.</p><p>And to top it all off? Musk’s beloved Cybertruck, the steel monstrosity that looks as if it were designed by a five-year-old, is <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/technology/2026/nov/06/tesla-to-wind-down-cybertruck-production-as-elon-musk-focuses-on-robotics-and-ai">winding down production</a>. According to Musk, this isn’t because it’s an abject failure, but because he is channelling his energy into other things. “This is not a case of Cybertruck being unprofitable, as has been misreported by legacy media,” Musk <a href="https://x.com/elonmusk/status/2119691615774146614?a=pN3ISFVZZ-aU4_-TlJw&amp;s=20">tweeted</a> on Monday. “But rather that the opportunity cost of the complexity of Cybertruck is vastly outweighed by the value of incremental Cybercab production.” (The Cybercab is a two-passenger robotaxi.)</p> <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/nov/11/farewell-cybertruck-elon-musk-car-repellent">Continue reading...</a></description>
