<![CDATA[Irish Times Feeds]]>https://www.irishtimes.comTue, 17 Nov 2026 18:06:09 +0000en1hourly1<![CDATA[European shares fall as investors eye Nvidia results and Jensen Huang’s return hopes]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/17/european-shares-fall-as-investors-eye-nvidia-results-and-jensen-huangs-return-hopes/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/17/european-shares-fall-as-investors-eye-nvidia-results-and-jensen-huangs-return-hopes/Tue, 17 Nov 2026 18:03:39 +0000European shares fell on Tuesday as markets globally awaited Nvidia earnings after the Wall Street close and Anthropic’s initial public offering (IPO) later in the week for fresh clues on the durability of the artificial intelligence (AI) trade.

Investors are also assessing the fallout from Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang’s sudden exit last week and move on Tuesday to fuel a campaign from certain quarters that he be reinstated – saying he would be “honoured” to return to the helm.

The pan-European Stoxx 600 index closed down 1.8 per cent.

DUBLIN

The Iseq All-Share index fell 1.5 per cent to 14,796.32.

Kenmare Resources fell 8.1 per cent to €2.94 as the titanium minerals miner said that an Abu Dhabi suitor has been given an extra four weeks to announce a bid for the business.

Bucking the trend, Origin Enterprises rose almost 1 per cent to €4.24 after the agribusiness company reported 17 per cent revenues growth for the three months to the end of October on the back of surging fertiliser prices and outlined medium-term financial targets.

Heavyweight stocks like Ryanair, Kingspan and Kerry Group were out of sorts, falling 1.6 per cent, 2.3 per cent and 2 per cent, respectively.

LONDON

The UK’s FTSE 100 logged its steepest one-day percentage fall in eight months – falling 1.8 per cent – as investors shied away from risky bets ‌in advance of AI bellwether Nvidia’s results, while mixed labour market data left expectations of a Bank of ​England rate hike intact.

Traders see a roughly 90 per cent chance of a Bank of England rate hike in December, broadly unchanged after the jobs data, LSEG data showed

Imperial Brands fell 2 per cent after the tobacco maker said it will cut up to 4,600 jobs, or nearly a fifth of its workforce, ‌by 2030.

Heavyweights HSBC ⁠Holdings, down two per cent, Unilever, off 1.8 per cent, Shell, down 0.9 per cent, and Barclays, down 2.6 per cent, were among the largest approximate drags on the FTSE ‌100.

Burberry fell 3.5 per cent alongside a pullback in other European luxury stocks on fears that a ​renewed AI-related sell-off could erode US wealth creation and ​sap one of the sector’s few remaining growth drivers

EUROPE

European technology stocks fell 3.9 per cent, ​their steepest daily percentage drop since early February.

ASML, one of Europe’s largest technology companies, fell 5.3 per cent, while AI-related equipment makers Siemens Energy ⁠and Legrand lost 3.1 per cent and 1.4 per cent, respectively.

Deutsche Bank fell 6 per cent after media reports based on ‌leaked documents detailed the bank’s dealings with clients including Russian oligarchs, US president Donald Trump and the late financier Jeffrey Epstein.

Miners tumbled ​ months as copper prices were ​weighed down by worries over AI investments, a firmer US dollar and weak economic data from top consumer China.

Chemicals company Evonik rose 4.2 per cent after Bloomberg News ‌reported that BASF was preparing a new takeover offer for its smaller German rival.

NEW YORK

Wall Street’s main indexes were lower in early afternoon trading, pressured by healthcare stocks, while ‌technology shares traded mixed as investors awaited Nvidia earnings.

Anthropic maintained its proposed price range of $70 (€63.52) to $78 per share ​for its highly anticipated IPO in an updated filing on Tuesday.

While the AI lab is expected to set the final price on Wednesday in advance of its Nasdaq debut on November 19, Bloomberg News reported that it could price its offering at the top of that range or higher.

Shares of Nvidia were lower. Intel fell after ⁠Nvidia cut its stake in the company by 25 per cent.

Software shares ⁠were broadly lower, with Salesforce, Workday, Intuit, Microsoft and Adobe declining.

Health insurers were among the biggest decliners, with UnitedHealth and Humana each down.

Nike shares jumped as the sportswear giant said it is targeting about $5 billion in ​incremental revenue growth by fiscal 2031. – Additional reporting, Reuters

]]>John Locher<![CDATA[‘Plant mattered over people’: Construction firm ordered to pay manager €37,000]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/17/plant-mattered-over-people-construction-firm-ordered-to-pay-manager-37000/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/17/plant-mattered-over-people-construction-firm-ordered-to-pay-manager-37000/Tue, 17 Nov 2026 16:37:06 +0000A construction firm that had its “head in the sand” about paying wages, to the point that a senior manager was owed more than €30,000, has been ordered to pay him €37,000 for employment rights breaches.

Thomas McAuliffe, a contracts manager, secured the sum for constructive dismissal and non-payment of wages following complaints to the Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) after quitting his €112,000-a-year job at Cork-based construction firm Howley Contracts Ltd in January 2025.

He had been at the firm nearly eight years, but had faced an “unsustainable climate of unpaid wages” and “a series of broken promises” for his last two years, he told a tribunal hearing in August.

McAuliffe’s evidence was that during that time, he was issued payslips “populated with pay details” but with no corresponding bank transfers.

He was short by €25,604 in December 2023, he said. By December 2024, the deficit had grown to €31,722.77 in outstanding wages and a further €5,814.46 in outstanding expenses.

At the time, he said, he was building a family home, and the delays to his wages were threatening the project.

At a meeting on December 12th, 2024, the company’s managing director “committed to paying €10,000” before Christmas.

“This was not honoured,” McAuliffe told the commission.

His evidence was that the company was making a priority of repaying finance companies over “paying plain people”.

“Plant mattered over people,” he told the commission, and the company’s focus was to get back to “the halcyon days of having over 400 trucks on the road”.

He wrote to his bosses on January 3rd, 2025, giving his resignation, stating that because of the failure to pay the promised €10,000, his position was “completely untenable” because of the “substantial unpaid salary”.

He left and took up a job paying €32,000 less a year three months later, the tribunal noted.

McAuliffe said he received money from the firm after his resignation, but maintained he was still due €11,657.26 in unpaid wages and expenses at the time of the hearing in August 2026, more than 1½ years later.

Adjudication officer Patsy Doyle wrote in her decision, published on Tuesday, that McAuliffe engaged positively about his money only for the company to “renege”. It was the “last straw”, she wrote.

Doyle called the firm’s failure to attend the hearing into the case “unreasonable” and wrote: “I have not received a defence in any form.”

She concluded that McAuliffe “was forced to leave the employment and can consider himself constructively dismissed”.

She awarded McAuliffe €32,750 for the unfair dismissal, reflecting the 12 weeks he was out of work and his lower pay in a new job.

Doyle made a further €5,065.51 as compensation under the Payment of Wages Act – the value of the outstanding wages he had sought, less tax and payroll deductions.

]]><![CDATA[Who’s buying a home in Ireland? Here’s what the data says]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/17/house-buying-trends-in-ireland-deviate-from-the-narrative/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/17/house-buying-trends-in-ireland-deviate-from-the-narrative/Tue, 17 Nov 2026 05:00:00 +0000Despite the challenges and difficulties in the housing market, people are still buying their own homes.

August was the busiest month to date for mortgage approvals, with more people getting the green light from lenders to buy their own home – more than 5,000 in that month alone – than at any other point since records began in 2011. This is despite property prices continuing to rise – albeit at a slower pace than before.

When they do buy, they are doing so with surprisingly high deposits, chunky incomes and often on their own.

So what can we learn about who’s active in the property market from the available information? And does it point to a sharp division where a certain cohort is locked out of the market, and those who can buy can well afford to do so?

More people continue to own their own home in Ireland, as opposed to renting, than might be expected. Yes, the figures remain lower than at their peak, but they haven’t fallen off a cliff as much as commentary might suggest.

According to figures from Eurostat, the home ownership rate in Ireland in 2025 was 70.9 per cent, up from 69.3 per cent in 2024, and 69.4 per cent in 2023. While this remains some way off the peak of almost 80 per cent in 2000, it puts us about mid-table in European terms.

As our table shows, in central European countries such as Romania and Poland, home ownership is as high as 93 per cent.

Irish house prices rising 14% faster than incomes, or double EU average

Ireland is closer to countries such as Spain (73.6 per cent), Portugal (71.2 per cent) and Greece (69.4 per cent). And above countries such as France and Germany, where home ownership rates continue to slide – from 64.7 per cent in 2021 to 61.4 per cent in 2025 in the case of France, and from 49.1 per cent to 47.2 per cent in the case of Germany. The UK has a home ownership rate of about 65 per cent for 2025.

Census 2022 data does suggest that, in Dublin, home ownership has fallen faster. And data from the ESRI has revealed that home ownership in Ireland is more concentrated among an older age group. Close to 80 per cent of people over the age of 40 own their own home, compared with less than a third of those younger than 40.

If that trend continues, overall home ownership figures are likely to fall.

Deposits

One perhaps surprising aspect is that while property prices continue to rise, first-time buyers are still bringing considerable downpayments to the table when they buy.

Central Bank figures show that the average price paid by first-time buyers in 2025 was a hefty €408,224, up from €385,385 a year earlier. And yet the mean loan-to-value was 79.8 per cent. That means these buyers are bringing a deposit of just over 20 per cent to fund the home purchase.

Even assuming many first-time buyers availed of Help to Buy at the maximum of 10 per cent of the purchase price, the average buyer still had their own deposit of 10 per cent.

Second-time buyers

Those trading up (or possibly down) continue to pay more for their homes, with the average property value up by 6 per cent to €605,528 between 2024 and 2025. However, the average loan size on these purchases is being held in check thanks to the equity or other savings second-time buyers are bringing to the transaction.

Central Bank figures show that, last year, the average loan-to-value for second and subsequent buyers stood at 65.7 per cent, indicating that buyers were able to put down just over a third of the purchase price in cash – or some €207,700, based on the average purchase price. While some of this is likely down to equity coming from the sale of their current home, it is still a hefty deposit.

In 2017, these buyers were borrowing more – an average loan-to-value of 67.1 per cent – though, with an average purchase price of €417,429 back then, this meant a deposit of just €137,334.

Owning a home now out of reach, most young people believe – research

Purchaser age

There is a narrative that people are buying much later in life, but that is not supported by the data. Figures show that this hasn’t really changed in recent years.

Data from the CSO indicates that the average age of a property purchaser last year was 40 – the highest on record. However, when we break it down by first-time buyers and previous homeowners, there is no trend of ageing buyers.

Of those who do buy, the average first-time buyer age is still 35, according to the Central Bank – unchanged since 2021, and only a slight increase on 2017, when it was 34. Although this is up significantly from 29 in 2006, it is holding steady – at least for now.

When it comes to those making their second or subsequent purchase, the mean age was 42 in 2025. Again, this has increased only slightly, up from 41 in 2017.

Incomes

Given the sharp rise in property prices, it’s no surprise that those who are buying have higher incomes than in the past.

Central bank figures show that first-time buyers had an average income of €70,230 in 2017; by 2025, this had jumped to €94,957. When it comes to existing homeowners moving to a new home, the average 2017 income of €111,223 had risen to €146,281 by 2025.

And of course, you’re going to need a lot more than the average to buy in certain parts of Ireland. With a median price of €851,500 in Blackrock, south Co Dublin, you will need an income of about €191,000 to buy there, based on a lending multiple of four times income.

Another sign of affordability – at least for the cohort that is buying – is that while there is scope to borrow up to four times income under Central Bank rules (and potentially more with an exemption), the figures show that first-time buyers have a typical loan-to-income ratio of just 3.5 times, based on a typical income of almost €95,000. Still, this has increased on 2017 however, when it was just three times income for first-time buyers.

More established buyers are borrowing just 2.7 times income, on average – up slightly on 2.5 times back in 2017.

Nonetheless, incomes are not rising as fast as property prices. Since 2017, for example, second-time and subsequent buyers had seen their average income increase by some 31 per cent – but the average price paid for a property has risen by 45 per cent.

That ties in with recent figures from Eurostat, which show that the growth in house prices relative to income in Ireland between 2015 and 2025 was about 14.4 per cent – more than double the EU average (6.8 per cent).

‘Price growth is moderating’: Irish estate agents give their views on new homes market in 2026

Single buyers

Of those who did buy a home in 2024, Central Statistics Office figures show that there were almost the same number of single men as single women – at about 9,500 purchases each, accounting for about 20 per cent each (or 40 per cent combined) of property purchases that year.

In some parts of the State, there are greater numbers of single women buyers than men – even in very pricey areas.

Take Dún Laoghaire in south Co Dublin, for example. Figures show that about 14 per cent of homes there in 2024 were bought by single men; women buying on their own accounted for a substantially higher proportion, at almost 20 per cent.

In other counties, the opposite is in evidence. In Donegal, for example, 27.8 per cent of buyers were single men compared with 18.3 per cent women. And in Longford, which has some of the cheapest house prices countrywide, single male buyers accounted for 31.4 per cent of purchases compared with 17.1 per cent by single women.

New arrivals

One element behind such robust home ownership figures is the tendency for new immigrants moving to Ireland to buy their own homes.

The latest official figures are from the census in 2022. These show that of those who bought property, 76 per cent were Irish citizens – even though Irish citizens make up 88 per cent of the general population; 11 per cent had citizenship elsewhere in the EU (6 per cent of general population); 7 per cent were Asian citizens (2 per cent of general population); and just 2.1 per cent were from the UK (1.6 per cent of population).

The number of international buyers has likely increased since.

]]><![CDATA[Grocery inflation reaches 6% in fresh blow to Irish households]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/16/grocery-inflation-reaches-6-in-fresh-blow-to-irish-households/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/16/grocery-inflation-reaches-6-in-fresh-blow-to-irish-households/Mon, 16 Nov 2026 14:04:30 +0000Irish households faced more financial pressure in recent weeks as grocery inflation jumped sharply to 6 per cent, up from a rate of less than 4 per cent just two months ago.

The latest figures from Worldpanel by Numerator also suggest the rate at which prices are climbing in Irish supermarkets has gone up by 1.3 per cent since the last tranche of research was published last month.

If inflation was to be maintained at the current rate over the next 12 months, a household that spends €200 a week on groceries could expect to spend more than €600 more over the next year than they did in 2025.

The figures come following almost four years of sustained increases in Irish supermarkets and mean that an average household will be spending as much as €4,000 more on groceries over the course of a year compared with the years leading up to the end of 2021.

Sparked by the US-Israeli war in Iran, elevated energy prices have fed through to food and other goods throughout the year. Published on Monday, new Central Statistics Office figures revealed an 8 per cent jump in agricultural input prices in the 12 months to the end of September, driven by double-digit increases in motor fuel and fertiliser prices.

Tricks of the trade: 12 ways supermarkets get us to spend money

“Grocery price inflation continued to increase after slowing over the summer,” said Worldpanel’s head of retail Eimear Faughnan.

“Household budgets are taking a hit as home-heating and fuel prices continue to rise with the arrival of colder weather in October. Grocery sales growth slowed this period as shoppers keep a close eye on prices and their spending at the tills.”

The Worldpanel figures suggest that take-home sales in Ireland increased by 3.9 per cent over the four weeks to November 1st.

Faughnan noted that shoppers continued to manage rising cost with own-label ranges adding more packs to baskets than branded products but brands still lead on value, holding 50.7 per cent share, with sales up 10.6 per cent on last year.

Shoppers filled baskets with ingredients for home-cooked meals and spent an additional €6.2 million on fresh foods, with savoury home-cooking ingredients climbing by €2.4 million and sweet home-cooked baking by €1.9 million.

Halloween and early preparations for Christmas kept branded chocolate confectionery and sweets in baskets, with spending up by a combined €26.7 million. Branded wine also boosted its performance, with almost €27.7 million in additional spend over the latest 12 weeks.

Over the latest 12 weeks, Dunnes continued to lead the pack with 24.9 per cent market share and sales growth of 6 per cent year on year while Tesco had 24 per cent of the market with sales growth of 5.4 per cent.

SuperValu continues to lag behind the top two with 18.9 per cent of the market and sales up 1.9 per cent.

Lidl holds 14.1 per cent of the market with sales up 4.8 per cent on last year while Aldi had a share of 10.9 per cent with sales up 0.8 per cent.

]]>Dan Dalton<![CDATA[Traveller caravans leave Kerry Group property, court hears]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/17/traveller-caravans-leave-kerry-group-property-court-hears/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/17/traveller-caravans-leave-kerry-group-property-court-hears/Tue, 17 Nov 2026 17:28:45 +0000A number of Travellers’ caravans which parked on property owned by the Kerry Group in Naas, Co Kildare, have left, the High Court heard.

Two weeks ago, the caravans moved into part of the Millennium Park, next to Chestnut House, owned by Ravelin Ireland Ltd.

Ravelin obtained an interim injunction preventing trespass, and on Wednesday last, the caravans moved out of its property.

But, the court heard, they did a U-turn, and went into a part of the park owned by Kerry Group International Services Ltd.

Two caravans went into a car park after removing a barrier at an emergency entrance, but left when a security man approached them.

The caravans, along with a number of others, pulled up on grass verge/footpath/cycleway space on the approach road, which is also owned by Kerry.

On Friday, Kerry Group obtained an injunction ordering them to leave.

On Tuesday, Joe Jeffers, counsel for the company, told Judge Brian Cregan they had vacated the property on Sunday.

Counsel asked that the interim injunction be extended for six months as had already been done in the Ravelin case to prevent re-entry and further trespass.

The judge adjourned the matter to next April, with the interim injunction to continue until then.

]]>Picture: Finbarr O'Rourke<![CDATA[Judge orders redactions in ‘personalised’ affidavit statements in Flatley dispute]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/crime-law/courts/2026/11/17/judge-orders-redactions-in-personalised-affidavit-statements-in-flatley-dispute/https://www.irishtimes.com/crime-law/courts/2026/11/17/judge-orders-redactions-in-personalised-affidavit-statements-in-flatley-dispute/Tue, 17 Nov 2026 17:02:58 +0000Lord of the Dance star Michael Flatley has succeeded in having statements in written evidence sworn by his former financial adviser and former solicitor struck out.

At the High Court, Judge Eileen Roberts made the decision in a pretrial motion in a case centred on €200,000 lodged in court in the wake of a dispute over Flatley’s Cork mansion, Castlehyde.

Flatley’s legal team had last month applied to the court for certain paragraphs in an affidavit sworn by the entertainer’s former solicitor Maxwell Mooney relating to Flatley be excluded, along with an affidavit of Flatley’s former financial adviser Des Walshe.

In her judgment, the judge noted Flatley contended Mooney and Walshe “wrongfully deployed legally privileged material in their affidavits in this application in a manner that is prejudicial to Mr Flatley’s position including in the Castlehyde proceedings”.

The judge said Flatley also says that Mooney’s affidavits and those of Walshe “contain scandalous and irrelevant personal material serving no apparent purpose other than to embarrass Mr Flatley”.

In turn, Mooney has submitted that Flatley and another person have in their affidavits introduced irrelevant, scandalous and inaccurate material intended to embarrass Mooney including in a professional capacity, the judge said. He also submitted that Flatley had waived legal privilege, which Flatley denied.

The judge said Mooney’s motion seeking to charge the sum of €200,000 has generated a significant and disproportionate amount of documentation from both sides relative to the size and complexity of the charging claim advanced.

The judge said it was reasonable for Mooney to confirm the basis on which he took instructions from Walshe on behalf of Flatley, but it was not appropriate for Mooney to exhibit Walshe’s affidavit in his own affidavit and she said it should be removed.

Referring to the Walshe affidavit, the judge said that much of it was entirely irrelevant to the application by Mooney for a charge over the lodged money.

She said it was at times highly personalised.

“In my view it is most certainly gratuitous as there was no need to mention many of the more personal details in order to deal with the claims made by Mr Mooney,” the judge said.

She said she believed that many of the averments “are also vexatious in that they are designed to and would cause distress to the named individuals in an entirely unnecessary manner and for no purpose relevant to this claim”.

The judge added: “Mr Flatley just as any other individual involved in legal proceedings is entitled to fair process. He does not lose that entitlement simply because he is a household name and there will be a level of interest generated in the media and elsewhere about his personal and business affairs.”

The judge said that Walshe’s affidavit “refers to and discloses privileged advices relevant to the Castelhyde Proceedings over which material Mr Flatley continues to assert privilege”. The judge directed certain paragraphs be struck out from the Walshe affidavit.

The judge said the amendments decided by the court can be applied by way of redaction to the existing sworn affidavits.

These redacted versions of the affidavit should be used for the substantive charging application before the court, which will be heard by another judge next month, the judge said.

]]><![CDATA[Can I buy PRSI credits voluntarily to boost an Irish State pension?]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/17/can-i-buy-prsi-credits-voluntarily-to-boost-an-irish-state-pension/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/17/can-i-buy-prsi-credits-voluntarily-to-boost-an-irish-state-pension/Tue, 17 Nov 2026 05:00:00 +0000Given you answered a question about the UK’s national insurance buyback, can I ask a related question: Does such a facility exist in Ireland?

“The global Microsoft outage is a stark reminder of how heavily we rely on a handful of Big Tech providers,” said Rob Demain, chief executive of UK-headquartered cyber security firm e2e-assure. “Its worldwide reach suggests the cause isn’t regional, and points to a software fault or a surge in network traffic rather than a localised failure.”

The outage is not the first to hit Microsoft’s customers in recent years. Users suffered similar disruption in July 2024, when a defect in a software update from cyber security provider CrowdStrike affected devices running its Windows operating system, causing one the biggest IT outages.

While Microsoft said at the time that this represented less than 1 per cent of all Windows machines, it took days for some customers to regain access and led to the cancellation of about 10,000 flights worldwide.

Although Microsoft has said the outage was not caused by a cyber attack, security officials have advised that cyber criminals would seek to take advantage of the disruption.

Demain at e2e-Assure added that with the cyber security management platform Microsoft Defender also down, corporate security teams had less ability to identify potentially malicious activity. “That is an ideal window for cybercriminals to operate unnoticed,” he said.

]]>Noreen M O Shea<![CDATA[Tribunal ruling sinks boat captains’ claims against marine staff agency]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/16/tribunal-ruling-sinks-boat-captains-claims-against-marine-staff-agency/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/2026/11/16/tribunal-ruling-sinks-boat-captains-claims-against-marine-staff-agency/Mon, 16 Nov 2026 19:30:24 +0000A tribunal has found it has no jurisdiction to hear unfair dismissal claims pursued by two survey vessel captains against an employment agency which supplied staff to the national sea floor mapping project.

The Workplace Relations Commission (WRC) has rejected complaints by skippers Peter Cullen and Roy Jackson under the Unfair Dismissals Act 1977 against Dún Laoghaire Powerboat School Ltd, ruling both men were in fact employees of the Geological Survey of Ireland (GSI).

GSI, the State agency in charge of Infomar – a 20-year project that started in 2006 to map the sea floor around Ireland – had not been a party to the proceedings at the WRC.

At a hearing last December, adjudication officer Patricia Owens noted a preliminary objection from Dún Laoghaire Powerboat School to the effect that the men were not employees and therefore lacked standing to pursue the complaints against the firm.

The firm, a registered employment agency based at the south Dublin port, maintained the skippers were sole traders being paid by invoice for skippering Infomar survey vessels, and that it had contracts in place giving effect to this arrangement.

Jim Keegan, the powerboat school’s spokesman at the hearing, said it had contractual agreements in place with Cullen and Jackson as “sole traders or as a company” and that they had been paid in line with these contracts on foot of invoices.

“At no point have we paid PAYE or PRSI in terms of Mr Jackson or Mr Cullen,” Keegan said, adding that Cullen included VAT on his invoices.

Keegan told the tribunal that on foot of GSI tenders, the powerboat school won a series of one-year contracts starting in 2023 “to supply staff – skippers, surveyors, data processors” for the marine survey programme.

“They may have had someone from the GSI contact them with the possibility of employment – sorry, I shouldn’t say that word – the possibility of a contract,” Keegan said.

“The only contact we would have had is by email; we would have had people recommended to us and issued a contract if we’re satisfied they’re suitable for a position,” he said.

Keegan said the company was aware Cullen was a previous contractor with the GSI.

Leanne Fox, who represented both of the skippers, said the contracts were “bogus”.

Cullen, she said, had worked “directly for GSI” on the Infomar mapping operations “doing exactly the same job”.

“They forced him to go out to the powerboat school; he was then forced to sign the contract that was presented to them,” she said.

In her decisions on the men’s cases, published today, Owens found both Cullen and Jackson were “integral” to the Infomar project as vessel skippers.

Neither were “free to substitute” another worker instead of doing the work themselves, a key determining factor in the legal test for determining employment status.

It was clear, she added, that the time and place of the work were determined by the Geological Survey of Ireland.

The State agency, and not the powerboat school, provided the survey vessels used for the Infomar work, she added.

Owens found that Cullen and Jackson were agency workers – with the Dún Laoghaire Powerboat School being the employment agency, and GSI being the hirer or employer.

Capital gains tax in Ireland is payable on gains made on the sale of assets. The key date, according to the legislation, is when the gains are realised.

The policy direction is clear. The National Planning Framework requires at least half of new housing in Dublin, Cork, Limerick, Galway and Waterford to be accommodated within their existing built-up areas. Government housing policy envisages more than 300,000 additional homes by 2030. Yet the places where we most want development to occur are frequently the most difficult and costly places in which to build.

Former industrial land, docklands, railway lands, redundant institutional sites and ageing inner-city districts often require land assembly, demolition, remediation, new streets, water and electricity infrastructure, schools, parks and public transport before substantial housing can be delivered.

Ireland therefore faces a fundamental contradiction. Planning policy is attempting to pull development inward while economics and infrastructure constraints continue to push it outwards.

This is why Copenhagen matters. Copenhagen’s remarkable transformation was not achieved primarily through enormous public subsidy. Its real innovation was institutional. Beginning in the 1990s, the Danish state and Copenhagen municipality brought substantial public landholdings into commercially managed development corporations, ultimately consolidated into CPH City & Port Development. These organisations combined public ownership with commercial discipline.

Public land was not simply sold to generate once-off receipts. It was treated as a strategic capital asset.

Planning increased its development potential. Infrastructure, particularly the Metro, increased its accessibility. That increased its value. The corporation could then borrow against that value, develop or lease land, enter joint ventures with private developers and pension funds, and recycle the proceeds into further infrastructure.

The sequence was straightforward. Public land was identified, comprehensive planning was undertaken, followed by infrastructure investment. This increased land value, which enabled development, value capture and reinvestment. It became what the Brookings Institution described as a virtuous cycle.

Perhaps the most important lesson is that Copenhagen put infrastructure in advance of development rather than waiting for development to justify infrastructure afterwards. The Metro fundamentally altered the value and attractiveness of Ørestad and later development areas.

More than 700 homes planned for Digital Hub lands in Dublin 8

Just as importantly, Copenhagen did not sell valuable public land prematurely. During the financial crisis it resisted pressure to dispose of assets cheaply. It used leases, rental income and joint ventures as well as outright sales, allowing the public sector to retain a share of the long-term value created by its own investment.

Ireland should not attempt to copy Copenhagen literally. But we should urgently apply its underlying principles. The striking fact is that Ireland already possesses most of the necessary instruments. We have the Land Development Agency (LDA), extensive publicly owned land, big housing programmes, regeneration funding, the €1 billion Housing Infrastructure Investment Fund, Croí Cónaithe, cost-rental supports, the Living City Initiative, vacancy and refurbishment schemes, the Residential Zoned Land Tax and planned investment in rail, Luas, MetroLink, water and energy infrastructure.

Our primary problem is no longer the absence of policy instruments. It is fragmentation. Land may be owned by one State body, planning controlled by another, transport delivered by another, water infrastructure provided by another and electricity capacity determined elsewhere. Housing funding and regeneration and transport investment are too often administered as separate programmes rather than assembled around the development of entire places. That must change.

Each of Ireland’s five cities should identify a small number – perhaps three to five – of strategic regeneration and transport-oriented development areas capable of accommodating housing and employment at genuinely significant scale.

For each city, the local authority and LDA should establish a long-term development partnership into which appropriate State lands can be transferred, leased or pooled. These partnerships should have multidisciplinary teams combining planning, property, infrastructure, finance and commercial development expertise.

Their purpose should not be to add another administrative layer. It should be to bring together functions that are at present divided. The first priority must be land assembly. Fragmented ownership should not be allowed to dictate the shape of our cities.

Bad news for Government: inflation triggers slowdown in construction

The second must be infrastructure certainty. Water, wastewater, electricity and public transport must be programmed before development rather than repeatedly emerging as reasons why development cannot proceed.

The third must be planning certainty. Detailed area plans should settle streets, densities, building heights, schools, parks, transport and infrastructure in advance. Development complying with those plans should then move through a substantially simpler consent process. Urban Development Zones under the Planning and Development Act 2024 could eventually become particularly valuable in this regard, but their potential must be translated rapidly into an operational system.

Most importantly, Ireland must rethink how it values public land. The maximum immediate sale price should not automatically be regarded as the best return to the taxpayer. Retaining land through long leases or joint ventures can generate housing, recurring income, infrastructure funding and decades of appreciation.

The same principle should apply to transport investment. MetroLink, DART+, Luas expansion and main rail corridors should be considered not merely transport projects but city-building projects. Where billions of euro of public investment create substantial increases in surrounding development capacity and land value, part of that value should systematically be captured for further infrastructure and affordable housing.

Time is becoming critical. Between now and 2030 Ireland must move from hundreds of disconnected schemes towards a limited number of big city-building programmes. During the 2030s, those programmes should mature into revolving investment systems in which the value created by one generation of development helps finance the next.

Deloitte’s housing hand grenade

Compact growth will not be achieved simply by putting higher-density targets into planning documents. Nor will our housing crisis be solved by repeatedly extending the edges of our cities. Successful compact cities require infrastructure, parks, schools, attractive public spaces, sustainable transport and places where people genuinely want to live. Copenhagen’s greatest lesson is therefore not architectural. It is institutional.

Ireland already has the land, the capital, the planning policies and most of the financial instruments required. What we still lack is a mechanism capable of combining them. Public land should cease to be viewed principally as property awaiting disposal. It should be regarded as strategic capital with which to build the next generation of Irish cities.

If we fail to make that change now, the consequences will be visible for decades in continuing housing shortages, worsening congestion, urban sprawl and missed regeneration opportunities. If we make it, Ireland has an opportunity to turn public investment into a permanent cycle of better infrastructure, more housing and stronger cities.

Tony Reddy is a member of the Irish Cities 2070 Group, and chairman of Reddy A+U

]]>AleksandarNakic<![CDATA[When human judgment is not all it’s cracked up to be]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/11/16/when-human-judgment-is-not-all-its-cracked-up-to-be/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/work/2026/11/16/when-human-judgment-is-not-all-its-cracked-up-to-be/Mon, 16 Nov 2026 05:28:00 +0000Human judgment is the future. At least that is the case tech bosses make to counter fears of an impending AI jobpocalypse. As work is automated, the argument goes, workers will be liberated from drudgery, free to enjoy their humanness and deploy the special quality that sets them apart from machines and animals: discernment.

“The things that make us human will become much more important instead of much less important,” Daniela Amodei, co-founder of Anthropic, said this year. “Understanding ourselves, understanding history, understanding what makes us tick – I think that will always be really, really important.”

As a human, I am in favour of this rosy future – or indeed, a future. But tech chiefs’ arguments often seem like marketing spin. Designed to flatter their audience (humans), making us feel special, insightful and evolved, it is far preferable to that other scenario they sometimes set out: the end of the world.

So, it has been fascinating to witness this much-feted humanness on full display over the past 10 days. By that I mean Jensen Huang, cofounder and until a few days ago chief executive of Nvidia, the US semiconductor group underpinning the AI boom, who has been unfaithful to his wife of more than four decades, and the mother of his two children, with a woman who is allegedly a Chinese spy.

In an age of anodyne press releases, seemingly spewed by GenAI, the one from Huang laying out his apology was striking: “I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry.”

Later came more evidence of that famous human judgment, this time from Donald Trump, who said Huang had “totally” denied knowing of possible sexpionage. “I really believe him ... When I heard about it ... I was amazed because I view him as a very high-quality person,” the US president said – before announcing the FBI’s investigation.

This was followed by new reports that Huang had an extramarital affair with a colleague, potentially breaching the company code of conduct. He resigned shortly afterwards.

Other tech titans have made dumb errors. Just look at Elon Musk’s reposting of conspiracy theorists, or the time he called the British man rescuing Thai kids from a cave the “pedo guy”. Some might say these pale in comparison to fruitlessly ploughing millions into Republican midterm campaigns, but at least his judgment seems calculated.

Every generation invents a technology that changes business. Today it is AI; when I started work, it was the internet, and long before that it was the typewriter. So it is reassuring to see that some things never change: an older man in a leather jacket is vulnerable to attention from an attractive younger woman, even as people increasingly turn to chatbots for companionship.

So much so that staff at AI companies have reportedly been warned about romantic approaches from spies. Even smart, successful people are fallible. Maybe more so because their record makes them feel invincible. Enron’s top team, after all, were always the smartest guys in the room.

The human frailty exposed by Huang’s behaviour brings to the surface other judgment problems. Chiefly, how did such a valuable company, with no chair and several loyal, long-standing directors, allow itself to become so dependent on one man, with no clear succession plan?

Accountability – from voters, the board or shareholders – has a moderating effect on the powerful, says Joris Lammers, professor of political psychology at the University of Cologne, who has studied the relationship between power and infidelity.

Like alcohol, “power has a disinhibiting effect”, he told me, making those in charge “less focused on threats ... more inclined to do what they want [and] more inclined to infidelity”. More so than even the opportunities given by business travel.

Employers and educators have spotted a gap in the market for humans to gain an edge over AI by trying to encourage workers and students to hone their analytical skills or become better people. PwC, the consultancy, recently launched a new critical thinking and judgment training course for 85,000 partners and employees to help “strengthen the human capabilities”.

Maureen Dowd: At this perilous moment, Donald Trump and Jensen Huang are letting us down

Having just whipped through a corporate training course purely to get to the end, I am not entirely convinced this is the solution.

Human judgment may not be all it’s cracked up to be, but I’m not ready yet to give in to our machine overlords. – Copyright The Financial Times Limited 2026

Initial UK assets will include Oaktree build-to-let apartment buildings in Bristol, Southampton, Walton-on-Thames and Farnham in England.

]]><![CDATA[The Cybertruck flopped, but investors are still buying Musk’s moonshots]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/16/the-cybertruck-flopped-but-investors-are-still-buying-musks-moonshots/https://www.irishtimes.com/your-money/2026/11/16/the-cybertruck-flopped-but-investors-are-still-buying-musks-moonshots/Mon, 16 Nov 2026 05:00:00 +0000Elon Musk is fond of making grandiose predictions. Delivering them? Well, that’s another matter.

The Cybertruck, Tesla’s futuristic pick-up truck – was once touted as everything from a workhorse to a vehicle capable of travelling on Mars – is facing the end of the road. Musk says production will be wound down around the middle of 2027, barely three-and-a-half years after the first deliveries.

In 2023, Musk said an annual sales figure of 250,000 was a “reasonable guess”, adding it “might be 500,000”. However, the Cybertruck flopped. US sales almost halved in 2025, to 20,237, and fell below 12,000 in the first nine months of 2026.

To some extent, grand promises come with the territory for entrepreneurs – nothing ventured, nothing gained, and all that. However, the problem for Musk is how often they fail to materialise.

A New York Times investigation earlier this year examined 602 public goals and commitments Musk made over the previous 15 years. Just 19 per cent were achieved on schedule. Another 35 per cent were delivered late, sometimes by years, or never materialised.

For a further 33 per cent, there was no public update or insufficient information to establish whether they had been achieved. The remaining 13 per cent had deadlines still in the future.

His record also worsened over time: nearly three-quarters of his 2015 goals were met on schedule, compared with fewer than half by 2020.

Of course, Musk has also delivered some remarkable successes, but it’s hard to disagree with the FT’s Lex column, which described the Cybertruck as a masterclass in “failing upwards”.

Tesla Ireland’s chief on selling more cars, self-driving taxis and robots in our homes

Shares have slipped in 2026, but Tesla is still valued at $1.5 trillion – a hefty 12 times annual sales, while its price-to-earnings ratio is well into the hundreds.

Why? Max Gokhman of Franklin Templeton, which owns Tesla shares, says Musk has shown that “after long periods of missing deadlines, a moonshot may materialise”.

Perhaps that’s what Tesla – and SpaceX, Musk’s other extravagantly expensive stock – are: moonshot stocks, where investors overlook repeated disappointments in the hope of an eventual breakthrough.

]]>Justin Sullivan<![CDATA[Tea clubs and americanos better for productivity than Zoom and WFH]]>https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/11/16/tea-breaks-and-productivity/https://www.irishtimes.com/business/economy/2026/11/16/tea-breaks-and-productivity/Mon, 16 Nov 2026 05:00:00 +0000Working from home at least part of the week has been a lasting effect of Covid for many office workers. It’s brought down the cost of commuting and made living a long distance from work more feasible. It’s provided flexibility for families around childcare. Overall, a third of the workforce now works from home either some or most of the time.

It’s not clear whether or not overall working time has been affected by this shift in work patterns. Data from employers suggest no change, while Labour Force Survey figures suggest men work on average an hour less a week than before the pandemic. However, because the respondents to that survey answer by phone, on behalf of all workers in their household, maybe some get that wrong.

Or possibly people include commuting time in perceived working hours, and that has clearly fallen.

While hybrid work is clearly popular – and more time in the office often resisted – the long-term impact on productivity is hard to establish. The common pattern, for example across much of the public service, of two days in the office and three days at home means that a minority of working time is spent being physically present with colleagues.

Engaging with people you already know well over Teams or Zoom video calls online is not necessarily a big challenge. Bringing new staff on board, and effective mentoring and managing of people who are largely working remotely, is much more difficult.

Hybrid working in Ireland expected to become less flexible over next two years, research suggests

“Sitting by Sally” was a traditional way for new workers to learn the ropes but it’s hard to pick up tips when Sally is working from her kitchen 30km away. It’s much easier to ask an experienced colleague what may be a trivial question if you run into them at the photocopier or pop over to their desk. New staff may be less likely to ask something they don’t know if it means sending an email or making a Zoom call. Where people are in or out on different core days, there may be some colleagues you never get to know at all.

So, given hybrid working, the informal bonds that help build a shared culture and knowledge in the workplace are now looser. One of the real casualties may be the cross-fertilisation of ideas and opportunities for collaboration.

The tea club was a key institution in the Department of Finance I joined in the 1970s. Those few rooms in Government Buildings that had a spare socket for a kettle were hosts to everyone in the section, from the typist to the assistant secretary general. While sport and political gossip provided much of the chat, in that 20 minutes a day there were also frequent discussions about economics that were like mini-seminars.

I learned a lot from colleagues who had studied abroad. Senior staff were generous with a rookie economist like myself when I floated maybe naive ideas.

How should a new recruit navigate a hybrid working system?

There was, initially, a different culture when I moved to the ESRI in the early 1980s. Like monks in their cells, researchers worked away in their rooms, and tea was delivered on a trolley lest you be distracted by chatting to colleagues.

I brought in a coffee percolator and would open my door at 11. The aroma attracted some exciting researchers who shared their ideas and insights over americanos.

Before long, the ESRI moved towards communal tea breaks, and over that period I can trace a growth in the number of research papers, and in collaborative authorship, as sharing ideas and pooling skills became the norm. The result was a big increase in productivity.

It’s not only in research or academia that working together produces more than working separately. Most workplaces require team working, sharing of experience and knowledge, and a positive culture of collaboration. They need people to spark off each other for new ideas, and that happens much more often in person than online.

From the employer side, hybrid working has allowed many to reduce their rent costs and office footprint. This often also involves moving to hot desking, where staff may have to find a different place to sit on each day they are in the office. It’s harder to build friendships and working relationships if you don’t know where Ciara will be sitting on a given day. Flexitime, where staff may only overlap for a few hours a week, also makes casual encounters with colleagues more difficult.

Hybrid working isn’t the problem, it is how to manage it

AI doesn’t do emotions and empathy, so coffee time becomes all the more important in helping build teams that enjoy working together. Six years after Covid, more time in the physical workplace might increase productivity.

The growth rate will mark an acceleration from an estimated 3.5 per cent or this year, the Irish business lobby group said in its latest economic outlook.

High household savings, strong balance sheets, investments under the National Development Plan and companies raising artificial intelligence-related (AI) expenditure will ensure the domestic economy is protected from wider international slowdowns, it said.

While headline gross domestic product (GDP) is forecast to fall by 0.8 per cent this year as exports are hit by US tariff-related volatility, the real domestic economy “remains in very solid shape”, Ibec said.

“High economic volatility continues to be a regular feature of global trade. For example, the recent drop in technology and semiconductor equities in response to US election news underlines the potential volatility in equity markets,” said Gerard Brady, Ibec chief economist.

“Despite this the Irish economy continues to absorb global disruptions from a position of real domestic strength. In just one decade, the Irish economy has navigated Brexit, tariffs, supply-chain disruptions, a pandemic and consecutive energy crises, yet underlying domestic growth has remained remarkably firm.”

Employment is on track to approach a fresh record of 2.9 million people at work next year, up from 2.84 million as of the end of June, with domestic demand poised to comfortably outpace European peers, Ibec said.

“We are now seeing the direct benefits of the global AI buildout feeding straight into our domestic growth. We have long seen strong growth contributions in this country from software, but are seeing a remarkable growth contribution from technology hardware,” said Brady.

“Capital spending on digital equipment has surged to nearly 2.5 per cent of national income, up from just 1 per cent two years ago.”

‘Mania’ for adopting AI to cut costs poses long-term risks, Ibec chief warns

The International Monetary Fund (IMF) said last month that the global economy “could soon test the limits of resilience”, as emergency oil stocks run low and government budgets become overstretched.

In its twice-yearly world economic outlook, the IMF said global growth had withstood the Middle East conflict better than feared over the previous six months.

It revised upwards its forecast for global economic growth this year marginally, to 3.1 per cent, compared with 3 per cent projected in its previous update in July. Next year’s forecast was unchanged, at 3.4 per cent.

   <title>Krim-Brücke bei Angriff schwer beschädigt</title>
   <description>Die von Russland erbaute Brücke zur annektierten Halbinsel Krim ist in der Nacht bei einem ukrainischen Luftangriff teilweise zerstört worden. Der ukrainische Präsident Wolodymyr Selenskyj bestätigte den Schlag gegen die Brücke und sagte, das sei eine Reaktion auf russische Angriffe auf die ukrainische Infrastruktur. Auch Russland nahm am Dienstag erneut Brücken und Energieanlagen in Kiew und in anderen ukrainischen Landesteilen unter Beschuss.</description>

<item rdf:about="https://orf.at/stories/3448327/">
   <title>Expertin sieht viele Gründe für Pagro-Fusion</title>
   <description>Was schon länger bekannt war, wird zeitlich konkreter: Bis 2028/29 sollen die Libro-Filialen auf Pagro umgestellt werden, das teilte die Schul- und Büroartikelkette am Montag mit. WU-Wien-Handelsexpertin Cordula Cerha sieht in der Fusion eine Reaktion auf das aktuelle Konsumklima: Pagro habe sich besser entwickelt und sei die stabilere Marke. Als Gründe für das Libro-Aus nennt sie unter anderem eine unklare Positionierung und starke Konkurrenz aus dem Bereich der Non-Food-Diskonter.</description>

Poland’s central bank has frozen outgoing transfers from the bank accounts of the Constitutional Tribunal (TK), citing conflicting claims over who has the authority to manage the court following a disputed takeover by a group of judges backed by the government.

The National Bank of Poland (NBP), which holds the tribunal’s accounts and is headed by a governor appointed under the former government, said it was not the bank’s role to determine which side was legally entitled to represent the institution.

Narodowy Bank Polski wstrzymał realizację zleceń płatniczych Trybunału Konstytucyjnego. Powodem jest spór o to, kto jest uprawniony do reprezentowania TK i dysponowania środkami zgromadzonymi na jego rachunkach bankowych – poinformował NBP.https://t.co/KXwEBL6j9k pic.twitter.com/0h90bPdTLO

— Rzeczpospolita (@rzeczpospolita) November 16, 2026

Last month, eight judges elected to the TK this year by the government’s parliamentary majority – but five of whom the opposition-aligned president, Karol Nawrocki, has refused to swear in – took control of the court.

They declared that the chief justice, Bogdan Święczkowski, and his deputy, Bartłomiej Sochański, both of whom were appointed to the TK under the former government, had been suspended for failing to fulfil their duties and launched disciplinary proceedings against them.

Święczkowski denounced the move as an illegal “coup d’état”. He has been backed by the court’s other six judges, also appointed under the former government. A few days later, Święczkowski submitted a statement to the NBP identifying himself as the sole person authorised to manage the TK’s accounts.

Later that week, after the newly elected judges held their first meeting and made several key decisions, the NBP said it had also received documents “indicating, in principle, other persons authorised to dispose of the funds held in the Constitutional Tribunal’s bank accounts”.

 

Meanwhile, Święczkowski also issued a legal challenge against the TK takeover at the Supreme Court, which on 10 November issued a ruling revoking the order to suspend Święczkowski and Sochański.

However, the validity of that ruling is disputed. Anna Korwin-Piotrowska, the judge who has claimed leadership of the TK, said that only the tribunal itself can decide on the issue. Disciplinary hearings for Święczkowski and Sochański are due to begin later this week.

Święczkowski, nevertheless, sent the Supreme Court ruling to the national bank as evidence that he remained the person legally entitled to manage the tribunal.

The dispute around Poland's constitutional court risks entrenching a system of legal dualism in which judicial authority depends on political allegiance rather than broad constitutional consent, writes @AleksSzczerbiak https://t.co/mtgutqSTQh

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) November 10, 2026

The NBP’s governor by Adam Glapiński, who was appointed under the former Law and Justice (PiS) government and is a longtime associate of PiS leader Jarosław Kaczyński.

On Monday, the NBP announced that it would suspend all payment orders relating to funds held in the TK’s accounts, citing “a set of documents, which mutually cancel each other out”.

“This means that payment orders are not executed, regardless of who initiates them,” the NBP said in a statement. “The National Bank of Poland has no authority to decide who is legally entitled to control the Constitutional Tribunal.”

Komunikat NBP (uzupełnienie) https://t.co/jkL8RmbXIr pic.twitter.com/M09O1KpDW6

— Narodowy Bank Polski (@nbppl) November 16, 2026

Finance minister Andrzej Domański criticised the decision, accusing the central bank of becoming embroiled in the political dispute. “The National Bank of Poland should safeguard its independence, including its political independence,” Domański said.

He added that the government would “explore all available options” to secure funding for the TK and ensure that it can continue functioning.

Justice minister Waldemar Żurek also condemned the NBP’s move, saying its “invocation of a non-existent document [the disputed Supreme Court ruling] to block funding for a constitutional body is…an attempt to protect an entrenched system”.

The historic St Mary’s Basilica in Kraków has hosted a holy mass for Michał Oksiński, the man who carried out the recent attack in the city and later died of injuries sustained in a shootout with police.

The six people who died in the attack and more than a dozen who were injured were shot by Oskiński on the square where the church stands, some of them just a few metres from its doors.

St Mary’s Basilica says that the mass is “an expression of the Christian faith in God’s mercy” and “in no way indicates justification for the crime”.

On the afternoon of 7 November, Oksiński launched his attack on Kraków’s famous market square, which was packed with locals and tourists. He shot at random from his car while driving through the square and surrounding streets before police managed to bring his rampage to an end.

Later that same day, the dead bodies of Oksiński’s parents and sister were found in his home. They had each been shot in the head while sleeping. Two days after the attack, Oskiński himself died in hospital.

On Sunday, Łukasz Wantuch, a former city councillor, shared a photograph of an announcement that there would be “a holy mass for the late Michał Oksiński and the deceased members of his family” at the Roman Catholic St Mary’s Basilica on Monday morning.

The church, built in the 14th century, is one of the most famous in Poland and dominates the skyline in Kraków’s historic, UNESCO-listed city centre. It stands on one corner of the market square, just a few steps from where some of Oksiński’s victims were shot.

“I won’t hide the fact that I find this somewhat shocking,” wrote Wantuch. He noted that the announcement referred to the “blessed memory” (świętej pamięci) of Oksiński. However, that phrase is standard usage in Polish to refer to someone who has died (the equivalent ot the English “late”).

“But perhaps that is what faith is about: praying even for a murderer,” added Wantuch. Among the more than 1,000 comments under his Facebook post, many agreed with that sentiment.

“The whole of Christianity is based on forgiving the unforgivable,” wrote one. “I don’t think anyone needs God’s mercy more [than Oksiński],” said another.

However, some others were critical of the fact that the mass was being held in that particular church among the dozens in Kraków. “It is the height of impudence that they’ll celebrate mass for him in the very church he murdered in front of,” wrote one commenter.

 

Later on Sunday, St Mary’s Basilica issued a statement, signed by parish administrator Father Mariusz Słonina, saying that the holy mass “is a private initiative of one of the priests, not of St Mary’s Parish”.

However, Słonina added that “praying for the deceased is an expression of the Christian faith in God’s mercy” and “in no way indicates justification for the crime, a lessening of the perpetrator’s responsibility, or a trivialisation of the suffering of the victims”.

Local news service KR24 reported that uniformed police officers were posted outside the church for today’s mass while plainclothes officers were inside, with one of them right next to the altar.

Three priests were present, including Słonina, who presided over the mass. Only around a dozen faithful were in attendance, with KR24 suggesting that many did not even seem aware for whom mass was being held.

Separate private funeral ceremonies will take place for Oksiński, his parents and sister, who lived in the town of Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski, about 160 km from Krakow. On Sunday, their family issued a statement asking the media to “respect the privacy, dignity and mourning of our family and loved ones”.

Meanwhile, police and prosecutors continue to investigate the possible motive behind Oksiński’s attack, which they are treating as a terrorist offence. Last week, the justice minister said that there were “very strong traces of right-wing extremism” in the perpetrator’s online activity.

Two police officers, Jakub Kulik and Artur Morański, who were seriously injured in the shootout that debilitated Okisński, have been recovering in hospital after undergoing emergency surgery.

Local police in Poznań told the Gazeta Wyborcza daily that they were searching for a young man dressed in black who is believed to be the culprit, but have so far not been able to identify him.

By Leo Greenberg

Speaking to Fox News in late October, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky admitted a widely known but uncomfortable truth: Ukraine needs its refugees back.

“We need 9.5 million people – who lost their homes, who are abroad, everywhere – we need them to come back to Ukraine…to rebuild their country,” he said.

Zelensky:

We need 9.5 million people who lost their housing, who are abroad everywhere — we need them to come back to Ukraine, just to live and to build their country. pic.twitter.com/Xu2Ld4eGOu

— Clash Report (@clashreport) October 21, 2026

Unfortunately for Ukraine, all signs point in the opposite direction: Ukrainians abroad are deferring or abandoning thoughts of return.

A large proportion of those refugees – almost one million of them – live in Poland, where Ukrainians, including migrants who arrived before 2022, have provided an economic and demographic boon. But their continued stay has also posed social and political challenges, as a country with no history of mass immigration grapples with the new reality of a sizable non-citizen minority.

This has left the refugees themselves in a state of limbo: torn between a homeland that wants them back, and to which many would like to return, but where conditions do not allow for it; and an adopted home where they have created new lives but where social tensions and logistical hurdles have meant persistent uncertainty.

A new reality sets in

When Solomiia Pischana, a Ukrainian woman in her late twenties, fled from Kyiv to Poland in the wake of Russia’s full-scale invasion in 2022, she hoped to go back that same year.

When Kyiv was secured by Ukrainian forces, a return seemed possible. In late 2022, Pischana started travelling back home to see family and friends. “I was really living between two countries. I thought a lot about going back.”

Yet quickly, a new reality set in on her visits: “In winter it became basically impossible to stay there – the constant explosions.” In Poland, by contrast, “everyone put the emphasis on helping me, on helping Ukrainians.”

In a photo essay, we look at the lives of three of the million or so Ukrainian refugees who remain in Poland one year on from Russia's invasion: Liudmyla, a mother; Vlad, an amputee soldier; and Viktoria, a high-school student https://t.co/kdOpEgt2LB

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 21, 2023

For many Ukrainians, Pischana’s story will feel familiar. When Russia launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine, Poland became the main waystation for Ukrainians on their way out. Millions crossed the border, and while many went on to other destinations in Europe and beyond, initially more than one million remained in Poland.

The Polish state reacted quickly, assigning more than a million special identification numbers for Ukrainian refugees – known as “PESEL-UKR” – and enrolling them in the same housing and benefits systems used by Polish citizens.

So too did Polish society, with a majority of Poles working in some way to assist Ukraine or arriving refugees, and many hosting refugees in their homes.

Around 77% of Poles have been involved in helping refugees from Ukraine, for which purpose they spent around €2 billion out of their own pockets, a new study by @PIE_NET_PL has found https://t.co/xWu8JWNMui

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 28, 2022

For Ukraine, the exodus of around six million refugees meant a raft of problems. Some 650,000 military-age men left the country, while schools had to figure out how to provide remote instruction for two million children abroad.

Most of all, the refugee crisis worsened Ukraine’s demographic challenges. Before 2022, Ukraine’s population of 42 million had already been shrinking and ageing. Now, Ukraine’s minister for social policy estimates that just 22-25 million people remain in Ukrainian-controlled territory. Two thirds of Ukrainian businesses are short of workers.

Initially, many hoped for a brief war. But, as the reality of a long, grinding conflict dawned, it became clear that Ukraine could no longer plan for an imminent influx of able-bodied adults: surveys by Kyiv’s Centre for Economic Strategies show that the proportion of refugees intending to return dropped from 74% in November 2022 to 43% in January 2026.

“Rather chaotic” attempts to connect with refugees

This reality has meant that, while Ukraine needs its people back, it also knows that it cannot compel people to return to a life defined by rolling blackouts and the ever-present threat of drones and ballistic missiles.

As a result, Ukraine’s efforts to encourage and support refugee return have been haphazard and limited.

Ukraine has one deputy minister, Ilona Havronska, who is armed with just 150 million hryvnia (13.1 million zloty, €3 million) in this year’s state budget to maintain connections with refugees abroad and support their return.

Havronska has sought to create a network of “Unity Hubs,” paid for by foreign governments, where Ukrainian refugees can confer with trained consultants about returning home. Such facilities have opened in Stockholm, Prague and Berlin, with the latter receiving 5,000 visits since opening in May.

⚡️Ukraine, Germany agree to open 'Unity Hub' for Ukrainian refugees in Berlin.

"This is a professional space that brings together community, business, and cultural initiatives," National Unity Minister Oleksii Chernyshov said.https://t.co/rlTq3MpOd0

— The Kyiv Independent (@KyivIndependent) February 15, 2025

So far, however, no hub has opened in Poland, whose interior ministry told Notes from Poland: “To be frank, the Ukrainian side, Minister Havronska, they haven’t approached us much about this recently.”

Ukraine’s other major effort, a digital platform called “Dodomu” (“Homeward”), allows users to make a return plan and check off items on a digital to-do list, such as transferring medical files, verifying IDs, and registering children in Ukrainian schools.

Since launching in June, Dodomu has been used by 4,500 people in Poland, of whom 600 have completed a questionnaire about their possibility of return.

Ukraine’s efforts to reach out to refugees abroad have been “rather chaotic”, according to Olena Babakova, a Polish-Ukrainian journalist and researcher who studies migration.

 

However, a survey by the UNHCR suggests that it may not make much difference: Ukrainian refugees ranked “support for return” as less important to their decision-making than security, economic opportunities, and housing in Ukraine. Nevertheless, for older refugees and those from now-occupied territories in eastern Ukraine, large numbers cited additional information as one of their key needs.

Valentina Bryl, a Ukrainian who has lived in Poland since before 2022 and is now an HR specialist in Wrocław, notes that returning to Ukraine would mean she would have to “start everything from the beginning – my job, my life. It’s not just about safety.”

So while Bryl says that she visits Ukraine often – taking the 25-hour rail journey from Wrocław to Kharkiv to see her husband, who is serving at the front – she hasn’t made use of Dodomu or thought about the Unity Hubs. She has no intention of moving back.

From welcome to wariness in Poland

Yet for the million or so Ukrainian refugees in Poland, as well as the hundreds of thousands of Ukrainian economic migrants who came before 2022, a growing consideration is not only the conditions in Ukraine, but also the environment they face in their adopted homeland.

Poland welcomed refugees in 2022 and has supported them since. It has also benefited economically from their presence, with Ukrainian refugees estimated to have raised national GDP by 2.4% in 2025.

Ukrainian refugees boosted Poland’s GDP by 2.4% in 2025, the equivalent of €21.5bn, according to a report by the UN @Refugees agency and @Deloitte

At the same time, their growing presence in the labour market had no negative impact on employment or wages https://t.co/lcsuIwBzpy

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) October 8, 2026

However, there have been growing social and political tensions. During the 2025 presidential election, even liberal candidates proposed restricting child benefits for Ukrainian refugees.

The eventual winner, right-wing candidate Karol Nawrocki, in one of his first acts as president, vetoed an extension of Ukrainians’ temporary protections, before signing a revised extension that restricted benefits.

Those political changes reflect shifting attitudes in society. A June 2026 report from the Institute of Political Critique (IKP) described last year’s election campaign as a “Rubicon”, citing testimony from Ukrainian refugees that the public environment had become more hostile and historical issues had surfaced.

Pischana told Notes from Poland that, while she is “surrounded by good people” in Poland, she has noticed that “old topics like the Volhynia massacre are coming up much more”, referring to the mass slaughter of Poles by Ukrainian nationalists in World War Two. “Just walking down the street and speaking Ukrainian, it’s started to feel a bit more dangerous,” she added.

Police data show that the number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland was 30% higher in the first half of this year than in the same period of 2025.

The number of reported hate crimes against Ukrainians in Poland is up 30% so far this year, police data show.

The figures come following recent high-profile cases of verbal and physical attacks against Ukrainians, who are Poland's largest immigrant group https://t.co/pcTsJddDz7

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) July 17, 2026

Myroslava Keryk, who leads Ukraiński Dom, a hub that provides services to Ukrainian refugees in Warsaw, told Notes from Poland that her staff have faced growing harassment.

She described a slew of AI-generated videos depicting them demanding Poles pay greater taxes to support refugees, as well as sexualised, fake accounts made of her employees on online apps.

Poland’s government has condemned the recent spate of hate crimes and accused the opposition and Nawrocki of stirring up such social vitriol. Meanwhile, it has begun preparing for Ukrainian refugees’ longer-term stay.

Ukrainian refugees’ current PESEL-UKR status is tied to the EU’s temporary protections, now set to expire in March 2028. So this year, the government introduced a new “CUKR” status, valid for three years of residence after it is granted. Some 75,000 Ukrainians have already submitted applications.

President Nawrocki has signed into law a government bill ending the special status granted in 2022 to Ukrainian refugees, who will now be treated on the same legal basis as other foreigners.

Nawrocki said he is "ending the era of unconditional privileges" https://t.co/BzY7wrdl49

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) February 20, 2026

This new status, however, is only a step on the path to long-term stability. CUKR, unlike most refugees’ current “UKR” status, counts toward the five years of legal stay required to apply for long-term EU resident status. However, its three-year duration means holders need to secure two additional years of legal protection in Poland before applying for long-term residency.

Polish state policies have not always made things easy for refugees. New restrictions on benefits and on travel outside of Poland have made refugees careful. Despite that, many appreciated the legal and logistical clarity of Poland’s approach, typified by the new CUKR status.

Refugees’ primary fears have concerned their social environment, not their legal status. Babakova put it neatly: “Ukrainians in Poland feel very connected to Ukrainian society, but not the state. At the same time, they have come to trust the Polish state, but not Polish society.”

The citizenship question

At the same time, a growing number of Ukrainians are thinking of obtaining citizenship, which would allow them to travel more freely and vote in Polish elections.

An August survey of Ukrainian refugees in Poland found that a plurality (35%) listed obtaining citizenship as the “most desired form of assistance” to make their lives easier.

In 2025, a record 19,000 foreigners, more than half of whom (10,000) were Ukrainian, were granted citizenship in Poland.

Poland granted citizenship to a record 19,135 foreigners in 2025, up 17% from the previous year and almost five times higher than a decade ago.

Over half of recipients were Ukrainians, followed by Belarusians, Russians, Vietnamese and Turks https://t.co/FoyWd5UPJx

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) May 15, 2026

But since then, Poland has moved to restrict access to citizenship – to make it “an earned privilege, not a formal certificate”, in the words of the interior ministry.

The plans include extending the required period of legal residence from five to eight years, requiring a loyalty declaration, mandating advanced knowledge of Polish, and introducing an exam on Polish history and values.

Pischana wants to become a Polish citizen: “I’ve thought that it would be logical […] I’ve lived for years in Poland. I know the language.” She added that her university thesis focuses on Polish history: she’s writing a comparison of Ukrainian and Polish songs with political or social themes, from the 1980s to the present day.

Kamil Kisiel, deputy director for the department of internal affairs and migration at Poland’s interior ministry, told Notes from Poland that the new citizenship laws, soon to be announced, will be tough: “For now, being more restrictive is the way to go, so that we can manage people’s expectations”.

The proportion of Poles who hold a negative view of relations with Ukraine has risen to the highest level ever recorded by state research agency CBOS

Meanwhile, the proportion who believe reconciliation with Ukraine is possible is at its lowest ever level https://t.co/YYBCFkVxNr

— Notes from Poland 🇵🇱 (@notesfrompoland) August 12, 2026

Kisiel was also up front that the Polish government does not envision many Ukrainians in Poland becoming citizens. No more than a few tens of thousands of Ukrainians have obtained Polish citizenship in the past decade, and those who arrived in 2022 are not yet eligible to apply.

Instead, Kisiel highlighted, “long-term EU residence is…the sort of stability people should expect”.

Karina, a Ukrainian woman who has been in Poland since she was 15 and did not want her surname published, says that she wants Polish citizenship as it offers “a chance to travel around the European Union, go to Spain. You can also go to America, because a Polish passport gives you visa-free travel; unfortunately, with a Ukrainian one you can’t.”

Head in Poland, heart in Ukraine

Barring a major change in the course of the war, Ukraine may even become one of the countries, including Ireland and Armenia, whose diasporas are as large or larger than their domestic population – a scenario that Havronska, the Ukrainian deputy minister, told Notes from Poland she is planning for.

At the same time, social tensions and citizenship restrictions in Poland reflect the fact that refugees are challenging Poland’s identity: since the eradication and movement of Jews, Ukrainians and Germans during and after World War Two, Poland has been a largely monoethnic nation, accustomed to one language, one faith, and one national identity. The approximately 1.5 million Ukrainians in Poland have changed that.

For Pischana, her head is in Poland while her heart remains in Ukraine, saying that she feels more attached to the culture of her homeland. “It’s a pity I can’t develop in my own country, because there’s room to do it there,” she says.

For Bryl, it’s been harder to keep close to Ukraine: “I have work, I have other responsibilities…You no longer want to read, you don’t want to get angry at some bad news”.

At the beginning, she said, she felt she had a fully Ukrainian life – just one that was put on pause. But, she adds, “when it’s already been going on for five years, and it’s still unknown how long it’ll go on, well, it’s hard to keep it on pause.”
