Prokurator z mazowieckiego wydziału PZ PK przedstawił posłowi na Sejm RP Władysławowi Teofilowi Bartoszewskiemu dwa zarzuty: przywłaszczenia powierzonych mu środków pieniężnych znacznej wartości oraz udaremnienia zaspokojenia wierzyciela.

Komunikat: ➡️ https://t.co/EXZ3NsovBh pic.twitter.com/Lmp2f3Bw2r

— Prokuratura (@PK_GOV_PL) November 10, 2026

The case dates back to before Bartoszewski had entered politics. In 2019, he became an MP for the centre-right Polish People’s Party (PSL). In 2023, after PSL became a junior partner in the current ruling coalition of Prime Minister Donald Tusk, he was made deputy foreign minister.

From 2004, say prosecutors, Bartoszewski was entrusted with managing the assets of Polish art collector and philanthropist Andrzej Ciechanowiecki, who was Bartoszewski’s godfather and a friend of his late father, Władysław Bartoszewski, a former Polish resistance fighter, Auschwitz prisoner, and later foreign minister.

From 2005, Władysław Teofil Bartoszewski, who has waived his right to anonymity in the case, also managed funds belonging to the Non Omnis Moriar Foundation, linked to the collector.

According to prosecutors, Bartoszewski used some of the money to buy and renovate three apartments in Warsaw between 2005 and 2006. From 2009, Ciechanowiecki began asking Bartoszewski to account for the funds, but he allegedly failed to do so and began avoiding contact with Ciechanowiecki.

 

In 2012, Ciechanowiecki and the foundation terminated their agreements with Bartoszewski and demanded the return of funds, say prosecutors. The following year, they filed a lawsuit demanding that Bartoszewski pay them around £1 million, 7.2 million zloty, €650,000 and $76,000, plus interest.

According to prosecutors, Bartoszewski then took steps to prevent the money from being recovered. A company owned by him and his wife sold three apartments in Warsaw, after which the couple disposed of their shares in the company. His wife also donated a property to their underage children.

“As a result of these actions, Władysław Teofil Bartoszewski and his wife possess no assets from which the creditor’s claims could be satisfied,” prosecutors said.

In March 2024, a Warsaw court ordered Bartoszewski to pay the foundation more than 13.2 million zloty, plus interest. Prosecutors note that the judgment is not yet binding as an appeal is still pending.

Od półtora roku sąd nie wyznaczył terminu apelacji w sprawie Władysława Teofila Bartoszewskiego — dowiedział się Onet. Sąd pierwszej instancji nakazał wiceministrowi spraw zagranicznych zwrot aż 13 mln zł, jakie powierzył mu jego chrzestny https://t.co/JzPwcJG4KU

— Kamil Dziubka 🟡🇵🇱🇺🇦 (@KamilDziubka) November 4, 2025

Meanwhile, in 2023, representatives of the Ciechanowiecki Collection Foundation at the Royal Castle in Wawel, which now holds the assets of Ciechanowiecki (who died in 2015), filed a notification to prosecutors of alleged crimes committed by Bartoszewski and his wife.

Earlier this year, the prosecutor general, Waldemar Żurek, asked parliament to lift Bartoszewski’s immunity so that prosecutors could bring charges against him. However, he voluntarily waived it on 6 October.

At the time, Bartoszewski told newspaper Fakt that he “absolutely does not feel guilty” and “the evidence confirms this”. He also claimed that there is “a political element to my case”, though he did not elaborate further.

Sejmowa komisja regulaminowa opowiedziała się we wtorek za uchyleniem immunitetu posła PSL Władysława Teofila Bartoszewskiego w związku z wnioskiem prokuratury w sprawie podejrzenia popełnienia przez niego między innymi przestępstwa przywłaszczenia mienia.https://t.co/ydA0jNNUQ8

— tvn24 (@tvn24) October 6, 2026

On Tuesday this week, prosecutors announced that they had charged Bartoszewski with misappropriation of funds of significant value – £1 million, €405,000 and 6,683,705 zloty – entrusted to him by Ciechanowiecki and the foundation. The offence carries a prison sentence of between one and 10 years.

A second charge concerns allegedly taking steps to prevent or reduce the recovery of money owed to a creditor. It carries a prison sentence of between three months and five years.

Prosecutors say that, on the same day, they “brought similar charges” against Bartoszewski’s wife and that both of the accused denied guilt.

Wiceszef MSZ Władysław Teofil Bartoszewski oświadczył, że nie przyznaje się do popełnienia zarzucanych mu przez prokuraturę czynów. Zapowiedział, że będzie bronił prawdy i swojego dobrego imienia "tak długo, jak będzie to konieczne". https://t.co/tGodfs9Gzi

— Interia (@Int_Wydarzenia) November 10, 2026

In a statement issued later on Tuesday, Bartoszewski issued a statement rejecting the allegations and saying that he “will defend the truth and my good name in every instance, for as long as necessary”, reports the Polish Press AGency (PAP).

“I am convinced that both the criminal proceedings and the ongoing civil proceedings will confirm my arguments and rights to my property,” he added.

“I consistently maintain that all actions related to the acquisition of the real estate were consistent with the original will of Andrzej Ciechanowiecki expressed at the time of their purchase, and the premises were intended to constitute permanent financial security for my family.”

Asked whether the prime minister would dismiss Bartoszewski following the charges or wait for a court ruling, government spokesperson Adam Szłapka said that the deputy minister “is currently on leave and decisions regarding this matter will be made upon his return”.

The annual march held in Warsaw to mark Poland’s Independence Day has passed through the city without major incident. This year’s event took place amid heightened security following the deadly terrorist attack in Kraków just four days earlier.

Hundreds of thousands of people, including President Karol Nawrocki, marched through the city amid a sea of white-and-red flags. The event, which is organised by nationalist groups, also acted as a display of unity among the right-wing and far-right opposition ahead of next year’s parliamentary elections.

Figures from the more liberal government, as always, avoided the march. Prime Minister Donald Tusk celebrated Independence Day hundreds of kilometres away in the city of Szczecin, where he issued an invitation to the opposition-aligned Nawrocki to visit his home for talks.

Zapełnia się rondo im. Romana Dmowskiego. Cała transmisja z #marszuniepodległości w @TV_Trwam pic.twitter.com/TvMHypx8gn

— Michał Rybka (@_MRybka) November 11, 2026

This year’s Independence March was held under the slogan “Polak w Polsce gospodarzem”, which translates roughly as “Poles are in charge in their own country”.

The slogan was chosen to “emphasise our opposition to foreign influences on Poland and underscore that Poland should be a nation-state without mass immigration”, said Rafał Buca, the march’s spokesman. “In Poland, Poles should rule – not some foreigners, not the European Union, not big corporations.”

On the morning of the march, the organisers shared an image showing Tusk as a puppet of European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen. “Time to cut the strings of foreign influence,” they declared.

Czas odciąć sznurki obcych wpływów i marionetkowych decyzji!

The main organisers of the march are associated with Confederation (Konfederacja), a far-right group that sits among the opposition in parliament. But it is attended by a wide range of people, from the mainstream right through to the radical right.

Leading figures from other opposition parties, including the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS), centre-right Development Plus (Rozwój Plus) and radical-right Confederation of the Polish Crown (KKP), were present, as well as Nawrocki, who last year became the first Polish president to attend the march.

A member of the march’s organising committee, Marcin Osowski, told broadcaster WNET that around half a million people were at today’s event. The municipal authorities, which are under the control of Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party, later put the figure at around 250,000.

That would make today’s Independence March the largest ever other than the one in 2018, when a broader event was organised to mark the centenary of Poland regaining its independence after World War One.

 

The opposition was aiming to show a united front amid their ongoing protests against the recent takeover of the constitutional court by a group of government-backed judges and ahead of next year’s parliamentary elections, at which they hope to unseat Tusk’s government.

“It’s about showing our strength and, at the same time, for this march to be a springboard for the election campaign,” said Jarosław Kaczyński, leader of PIS, during the march, quoted by the Niezależna news website. “Unity is important.”

Meanwhile, one of the leaders of Confederation, Krzysztof Bosak, told the crowd in a speech that, “while we have different experiences and views, under the white-and-red flag we form one community”.

“Next year, we must turn this community into an election victory…We must remove the current clique from power and form a pro-Polish government,” he declared. “We do not accept the violent takeover of state institutions. We demand respect for the law.”

However, Confederation’s other main leader, Sławomir Mentzen, shared a picture of himself at the march in front of a banner showing images of both Tusk and Kaczyński crossed out, alongside the word “Reset”.

While Bosak’s nationalist faction of Confederation is seen as more amenable to the idea of working with PiS to form a potential future coalition government, Mentzen’s libertarian faction is less enthusiastic about the idea.

Nadchodzi, nadchodzi Marsz Niepodległości! 🇵🇱 pic.twitter.com/o8Tkf8673G

In the past, the march has sometimes seen violence, with participants clashing with police. However, in recent years it has generally passed peacefully, and that was again the case today.

The city’s mayor, Rafał Trzaszkowski, who is a deputy leader of KO, said on Wednesday afternoon that, other than the illegal use of pyrotechnics (such as a flare held up by Mentzen), the march was proceeding without incident.

Local authorities in Warsaw had put in place additional security measures following Saturday’s terrorist attack in Kraków, in which a 24-year-old Polish man, Michał Oksiński, killed six people and injured over a dozen more by shooting an AR-15 rifle from his car.

Oksiński’s rampage was quickly brought to a halt in a shootout with armed police, and he died from his injuries on Monday. On Tuesday, the justice minister revealed that evidence uncovered so far shows “strong traces of right-wing extremism” in Oksiński’s activity.

There are "strong traces of right-wing extremism" in the activity of the man who carried out the mass shooting in Kraków, says Poland's justice minister.

Tusk, meanwhile, celebrated Independence Day in the city of Szczecin in northwest Poland.

“All of us, without exception, are responsible for ensuring that Poland remains strong, secure, free and independent forever,” said the prime minister. “Everyone who holds Poland in their hearts must understand that independence, freedom and a secure republic are a common good.”

Tusk noted that, since the recent crisis around the constitutional court broke out, Nawrocki has refused his offer to meet and discuss how to find a solution to a crisis that has pitted judges appointed under the former PiS government against those chosen by the current ruling coalition.

The prime minister today renewed that offer, inviting Nawrocki and his family to visit Tusk’s home in the build-up to Christmas. “We must be able to discuss things together, without bitterness, without hatred,” said the prime minister.

GRADE ONE action from Haydock highlights this weekend with stars of the staying chase division set to line up in Saturday’s Betfair Chase (3.00pm).

At the entry stage there is a strong-looking field of 13 still in contention, including last year’s winner Grey Dawning, 2025 Gold Cup winner Inothewayurthinkin and 2024 King George victor Banbridge.

With bits of rain around, but the outlook set to dry out later in the week, the ground shouldn’t be much worse than good-to-soft come race day.

The prospect of fairly sound going, along with many of the runners in here holding double entries, could lead to the race cutting up.

Grey Dawning has been targeted at this race again and is sure to be tough to beat for the high-flying Skelton team, but this is a deeper race than 12 months ago and he can be taken on at his current odds.

AFFORDALE FURY is only entered in this race, and it looks like he will take it in en route to a defence of his Savills Chase crown at Leopardstown next month.

His win in that race, where he beat Galopin Des Champs and Grand National hero I Am Maximus, is a standout piece of form and entitles him to plenty of respect.

Noel Meade’s charge goes well when fresh, having a record of two wins and a place from three seasonal reappearances, and should be ready to do himself justice here.

He’s versatile ground wise and looks worthy of each-way support at 9/1.

In the card-closing staying handicap chase (3.35pm), two catch the eye at each-way prices.

NEWTON TORNADO has an in-and-out profile, having won twice but pulled-up or fallen on three occasions last season.

On his return 12 months ago, he was extremely well backed and travelled with great promise before coming down at the fourth last.

He made amends in no uncertain style when a nine-length winner at Bangor and in January was an equally impressive winner at Doncaster.

Rebecca Curtis’ horses are running well, and if his jumping holds up, he should have claims here at 8/1.

The other of interest is Mark Walford’s CHASINGOUTTHEBLUES.

We tipped him up for the Scottish National in the spring and he ran a big race to finish fifth, when just running out of steam at the finish.

Earlier on last season, he chased home Newton Tornado at Doncaster and went on to win two races on the bounce following that, including over this trip at Catterick.

He returned this season when fourth at Perth last month, and that run should have left him spot on for this.

He’s been dropped a pound in the weights to 124 and is also now better off with Newton Tornado, so he looks solid at 10/1.

A word of caution on both runners is that they hold entries at Newcastle at the end of November, but with both already having riders booked for Saturday, it looks likely they will head to Haydock.

Over at Ascot, the best betting race looks to be the mares’ handicap hurdle (2.05pm).

There are plenty in here with chances, including highly campaigned mare, Jackie Hobbs, but at bigger odds LOVE OF NEYMORE could offer some value at 12/1.

She reappeared last month in a strong open handicap at Cheltenham, staying on well to finish fifth behind Seaniecon.

Being dropped two pounds for that run is somewhat surprising, and this looks easier back in mares’ company.

She’s consistent, goes on a range of ground, and looks a shade overpriced.

Affordale Fury e/w                         3.00pm               Haydock

Newton Tornado e/w                    3.35pm               Haydock

Chasingouttheblues e/w            3.35pm               Haydock

The chipmaker is set to release its first set of results since Jensen Huang’s dramatic resignation as chief executive last week, following reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected of being [...]]]>

Nvidia’s crunch earnings update on Tuesday could cloud the outlook for Anthropic’s blockbuster IPO later this week, analysts have warned.

The chipmaker is set to release its first set of results since Jensen Huang’s dramatic resignation as chief executive last week, following reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including one with a woman suspected of being a Chinese spy by US intelligence officials.

Nvidia’s update is expected to test Wall Street’s appetite for AI firms just 48 hours before Anthropic lists on the Nasdaq.

Nvidia’s shares have plummeted 13 per cent over the last week to $156.1 (£118.3), and tumbled 4.1 per cent in pre-market trading, with the stock losing more than a third of its value since its October peak.

The wider sell-off accelerated on Monday, with the Nasdaq 100 falling 2.7 per cent and the S&P 500 shedding 1.9 per cent, while Asian tech stocks also came under pressure overnight.

The update will be interim chief executive Colette Kress’ first opportunity to step out of the disgraced chief’s shadow and try to reassure investors that the AI chipmaker can continue its growth and ease wider nerves.

“Kress faces an unenviable task in restoring Wall Street’s confidence in the stock… this will be one heck of an earnings call,” said Neil Wilson, investor strategist at Saxo UK.

David Morrison, senior market analyst at Trade Nation, said Nvidia’s results had traditionally been a question of how far the chipmaker would exceed expectations, rather than whether it would beat them.

But Huang’s departure has introduced fresh uncertainty over its strategy, financing arrangements and relationships with customers.

“Could this be an opportunity to make public more unpalatable news? If so, how might that affect the Anthropic IPO set for Thursday, with pricing confirmation tomorrow?” Morrison said.

Others added that the outcome of the results will provide fresh insight into demand for AI stocks and the sustainability of spending, particularly that of Anthropic.

Knocking confidence

Anthropic’s debut is expected to be a “defining moment for the AI trade”, with the frontier model lab seeking a $1.4 trillion valuation.

But as the listing collides with Nvidia’s leadership crisis, coupled with a “relatively underwhelming earning seasons” for mega-cap tech companies, it has raised question of whether investors are ready to plough money into yet another AI bet.

“Nvidia’s earnings remain a critical piece of the puzzle,” said Daniela Hathorn, senior market analyst at Capital.com.

“Strong results could help reassure investors that the investment cycle remains intact, potentially supporting sentiment ahead of Anthropic’s listing. Conversely, disappointing guidance could intensify doubts.”

ING strategists warned that Nvidia’s results and Anthropic’s listing could also move government bond markets, reflecting how closely AI investment has become tied to expectations for US economic growth.

Clearly, sharp rises in the minimum wage and employer national insurance are unhelpful for businesses. As the Centre for Policy Studies has shown recently, the rise in employment costs since Labour came to office is double that of inflation. 

Milburn rightly suggests reducing employer National Insurance, lightening the burden of regulation and slowing the rise of the minimum wage. These are welcome as a starting point.

Secondly, tough love in the welfare system. The report notes that the massive rise in health and disability benefits among young people “far outweighs the actual change in ill-health and disability”. Many people are acting rationally: they get more money from the welfare system than through employment. Clearly something is broken, with both the impact on young people’s lives and the fiscal cost becoming a millstone around the country’s neck. 

Most people would agree that “work beats welfare” for almost everyone. Milburn’s solution, to create a new youth allowance for anyone under 25 claiming either PIP or the health element of UC, is radical and welcome. Young people will also have a duty to engage or face losing the rest of their benefits. This reform is necessary, and again similar to that previously recommended by the CPS, but it is far from clear that these  dramatic changes will get past the parliamentary Labour Party or their activists. 

Thirdly, the idea that government needs to get in the way again. I say this partly tongue-in-cheek; there are lots of areas where government can better help young people, and his proposals around apprenticeships and mental health provision are sensible. 

Unintended consequences

There are also some areas where I am genuinely conflicted, especially over an increased employment support programme. Currently, only £1 is spent on employment support for every £25 spent on benefits. Milburn wants to get that ratio to £1 of support for every £2 of benefits – hopefully by reducing the bill as well as increasing support. The review proposes that young people should be given guarantees of employment. Much of the work would be assigned to Mayors who will be responsible for ensuring opportunities are available in their local areas. 

On the one hand, countries like the Netherlands with low NEET rates do have intensive and localised employment support – people literally knock on doors and get young people into work or training. It makes sense to learn from that. On the other hand, previous British attempts at employment programmes haven’t been especially successful in moving large numbers of people into work. I just don’t trust the British state’s ability to design and run programmes that will actually be cost-effective. 

But there are some areas where his proposals will cost money, introduce complexity and have unintended consequences. For example, his proposals to pay employers £3000 to take on young people who are NEET will increase complexity and bureaucracy. It means employers may not take on the best person for the job. Likewise, asking the government to hire more young people or include youth employment in procurement contracts also introduces more bureaucracy. We also need much more accountability from Mayors who are going to be responsible for improving employment outcomes.  

Overall, I want to applaud Milburn’s ambition. He is trying to solve a big problem that has an enormous fiscal, economic and moral cost. However, I am concerned about the politics. We know that this Labour Party is highly averse to welfare cuts and loves government intervention. There is a risk that patchy implementation of this review will leave us with the worst of all worlds – pushing ahead with the increased government intervention and subsidy, without addressing the core incentives in the welfare system and reducing regulatory costs and taxes for business.

Daniel Herring is head of economic & fiscal policy at the Centre for Policy Studies

The creme de la creme of Silicon Valley are backing the return of Jensen Huang, but should Nvidia really take back the rogue CEO? We hear the case for and against in this week’s Debate

YES: The Nvidia board stated they have no reason to believe any secrets were compromised

Yes, but the evidence needs to clear him first. I won’t defend Jensen Huang for being unfaithful. He’s apologised, and I believe that is a private matter. Beyond his affair, at the time of writing there are a lot of unsubstantiated claims about his conduct.

We don’t know if Alice (the woman involved) was working for Beijing. Though internet memes would suggest otherwise, the US Justice Department has reached no conclusion on whether she is a Chinese spy. President Trump has said national security “was not put at risk”, and the Nvidia board stated they have no reason to believe any secrets were compromised. Worth noting, in 2023 MI5 said in the UK alone 20,000 individuals were targeted by Chinese agents largely through Linkedin to steal sensitive technological and industrial secrets.

The further claims about Huang having had affairs with staff members are unconfirmed and anonymously sourced. I condemn bosses who use their rank to pursue staff, but until it’s proven he did, it’s hearsay.

What I find interesting is, as Tech Crunch reported, “Huang has been a staunch supporter of open source AI”. His resignation may benefit closed source AI providers arguably trying to raise the regulatory drawbridge on open models.

Huang has been an incredibly influential figure in AI, co-founding Nvidia (in 1993!), betting on accelerated computing a decade before the AI boom, delivering AI chip market dominance and a valuation of $5 trillion in 2025, with the company investing in a significant percentage of the AI ecosystem.

The Nvidia board should finish its independent investigation to establish the facts. Did he abuse his position? Did he mislead his board? Did he break security or export rules? A no to all should see him reinstated.

Matthew Blakemore is the CEO of AI consultancy AI Caramba!

NO: Allowing Huang to return amid allegations would make it impossible to build an investment case for Nvidia

Parting is such sweet sorrow. But sometimes it is best. Jensen Huang became one of those business legends, growing a business and then spotting an opportunity to pivot and deliver even better returns for employees and shareholders.

It will have been traumatic for all concerned at Nvidia. But letting him return to the helm will just mean the dark clouds over the company take longer to dissipate. There are still too many unanswered questions around his relationship with Alice Huang and Nvidia’s China policy. Allowing him to return would mean that the company remains fettered to him as he is dragged in front of Congressional committees and hounded in the press, making it impossible to build an investment case for the company.

And what if he then has to leave anyway? This isn’t the way anyone thought the story would end, and it certainly seems like there isn’t much of a succession plan in place. But the only way forward now is for him to depart and for the company to move on.

Where does Nvidia go from here? Reclaiming market confidence is the first order of business, and that will take time. It also requires a commitment to transparency as the likely congressional investigation gets going. This is unlikely to be a short-lived process, but is the only way forward. Keeping internal talent is now the main concern, to avoid losing them to any competitor, either an existing one or a potential new rival. Nvidia is a $3 trillion company, and bigger than one man. Now it has to show that.

Chris Beauchamp is chief market analyst at IG Group

THE VERDICT

You may think being caught having an affair with a potential Chinese spy would be pretty hard to come back from, but stranger things have happened in Silicon Valley.

Currently, the petition to reinstate Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO has garnered more than 180,000 signatures. This includes the likes of Elon Musk, while Donald Trump also added his backing on Monday. 

Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick, who also signed, perhaps best summed up the campaign’s viewpoint: “He has erred, yes – to err is to be human – but I do not believe anything he has done rises to the bar of separating him from his company.” Nvidia’s shareholders, who have seen roughly $2 trillion wiped from Nvidia’s valuation since its October peak, may beg to differ.

Mr Blakemore is right that Huang has been critical to Nvidia’s success – that probably cannot be overstated. That over 8,700 of the campaign’s signatories come from Nvidia staff members themselves is also notable. But Mr Blakemore’s innocent-til-proven-guilty argument is hard to bear out when Huang himself has admitted to being unfaithful and said his colleagues “deserve better” from him. Those 8,700 staff backers also come from a staff count of over 42,000, leaving more than 33,000 employees unaccounted for in whether they support Huang’s return.

Taking back an ex can be oh so tempting, but most of us know it’s never for the best.

Robert Pattinson will be a great Bond – but his casting is bad news for Hollywood and its diminishing reputation for turning out new leading men

In new stills released today it has been announced that Twilight and Batman actor Robert Pattinson will be the seventh actor to officially drink freezing cold vodka and a tiny bit of vermouth to play orphaned, traumatised, fashionable, perennially middle-aged James Bond.  

Pattinson, who is 40 and rose to prominence through the five filmic adaptations of the Twilight Saga books, is a good choice. Firstly, he is a fine actor, with a range of indie projects under his belt, and an undefinable, hard-to-read quality that makes him alluring to Hollywood. You couldn’t quite pinpoint where he hangs out – the pub, a fine pile in the Hollywood Hills or a grungy gig – and it is that indie-to-mainstream crossover appeal has helped him sustain a career this long, developing the sort of CV former 007 producer Barbara Broccoli prefers (Daniel Craig, too, had been an indie darling before he picked up the holster). 

If you were to rank his undefinable, draw-you-in qualities, those smokey eyes that somehow seem both blue and brown but give nothing away would be at the top of the list.

Robert Pattinson is good for James Bond, bad for Hollywood

But Pattinson’s casting is less good for Hollywood. James Bond is surely the last role that could rocket an unheard of actor to the A-List, and not casting a burgeoning name is a missed opportunity. 

These days, it is incredibly hard to birth new stars. It was not this way in the 1990s when Pierce Brosnan was cast, and to some extent with Daniel Craig. Back then, putting a new face on the cover of The Sunday Times Culture magazine could make someone famous. I recall the former editor of that magazine telling me he’d once argued to give the cover to a little-known actor called Tom Cruise, and we all know how that went. But journalism doesn’t have a tenth of that power anymore – put someone on the front of a weekend supplement and they might generate a few hundred Instagram followers, but not a glittering Blockbuster career.

And then there are the nepo babies – the Anais Gallaghers, Hero Fiennes Tiffins and Rafferty Laws – clogging up the talent pipeline, making it even harder for new actors who don’t have famous parents to break through. 

The cinema also used to be a good platform for rising actors, but with fewer people going to the flicks at the weekend, and fewer films being made, producers are choosing safety by relying on bankable stars rather than newcomers (hello, R Patz). The death of the rom-com is a signifier of how people are mostly going to the cinema to see ‘event’ films these days, like new Batman, Spider-Man or James Bond films.

The power of franchises at the box office was proven again recently when Tom Cruise’s latest film, Digger, became one of the biggest box office disasters of the decade. Cruise’s casting alone couldn’t drum up interest from the public, illustrating how big stars can’t always guarantee box office return without the weight of franchises like Mission Impossible behind them.

One man who can, though, is James Bond. Ian Fleming’s spy could remedy all of these problems: I’ll put it simply: cast anyone to play him, and the cinemas will sell out.

I mean, not literally anyone, but cast someone good, and people will go. 

This clearly doesn’t play into the interests of new Bond owners Amazon – they just want a big name because a big name sells, especially after investing £1bn in new Pinewood studio expansion.

Not that former producers Barbara Broccoli and Michael G Wilson took this tack: when they cast a new actor as Bond, it was always a burgeoning name rather than an A-Lister. Daniel Craig had been in indie movies like Layer Cake; Timothy Dalton was more famous as a stage actor; Connery was a struggling working class actor from Scotland and Roger Moore a TV star rather than leading films. But look at the effect Bond had: Daniel Craig surely owes the critical success of his recent turns in Luca Guardagnino’s Queer and Knives Out to his role as 007.

Creating an exciting new star is high-on impossible these days – and Bond choosing not to take a punt on an upcoming name is a shame for Hollywood.

David Rees, chief economist at Schroders, branded the data a “clear warning shot” to Bank of England rate-setters ahead of a pivotal meeting in December.

“With inflation set to climb substantially in the months ahead, the recent strength of the labour market is making it harder to dismiss the risk of second round effects,” he said, referring to when the effects of an energy price shock become embedded in the economy through price rises and wage pressure. “It also strengthens the case for another interest rate rise.”

Economists are increasingly looking to the labour market as a key bellwether for the Bank of England’s next move amid the ongoing war in Iran.

Before raising the Bank rate for the first time in three years this month, Monetary Policy Committee members had for months pointed to the weak jobs outlook as a central reason for leaving their central interest rate unchanged.

Shrouding the picture was the continued drop in vacancies, which fell a further 22,000 to 690,000. Job openings dropped most among smaller employers, which ONS officials said had pointed to higher tax burden and energy costs for their decision to cut back on hiring.

Jeffries economist Modupe Adegbembo said the crosscurrents pointed to a labour market that was “stable rather than strong”.

“A labour market that is cooling slowly doesn’t justify the four hikes priced over the next year,” she added.

Swaps markets, which act as a gauge for the path of interest rates in the coming year, currently imply traders expect the Bank to raise rates three times before June and four times by November 2027.

“The Bank [has] a difficult decision at its final meeting of the year, just a week before Christmas,” Kit Reese, investment strategist at Quilter, said. “The Bank will hardly want to play the Grinch, but if inflation is still running too hot, another rate rise may be difficult to avoid.”

At a moment when travel feels like too much of an investment to waste on a one-note trip, South Africa makes a particularly strong case for itself. Few countries offer so much, so close together: safari, winelands, penguins, elephants, two oceans and one of Earth’s strangest botanical landscapes

To a vulture circling overhead, Earth Lodge is almost invisible. A short flight from Cape Town to Skukuza and a 45-minute drive through the savannah delivers you to almost nothing: just red dust, bleached grassland, and heat rising in waves from the ground. I’m led down a sloping cement tunnel and emerge into a cool, cave-like sanctuary. Water moves quietly over a natural rock pool, and beyond, an open wall frames immense, uninterrupted views of the Sabi Sabi Private Game Reserve.

This was once unbroken wilderness, a formidable stretch of bush deep in the Greater Kruger, close to the Mozambique border. One of the world’s great leopard strongholds, alive with traffic of the entire food chain, edged by the Sabie River, thick with crocodiles and hippos.

The ideal South Africa holiday itinerary

In 1979, South African investment banker Hilton Loon, and his wife Jacqui Loon opened their first lodge here and began building what would become one of Africa’s most enduring names in safari. Four decades, and four lodges later, Sabi Sabi has expanded westward to Cape Town, with the opening of The Claremont Boutique Hotel. It’s a natural evolution. South Africa defies a single landscape: to experience it fully is to move, within hours, from the shaded terraces of old wine country to the primal elegance of the bushveld.

Built at the turn of the millennium, Earth Lodge is no polished colonial fantasy. It has brutalist bones and recedes into the land with walls rendered from the very earth excavated to create them. Inside, felled trees are repurposed as furniture, with animal hide warming the slate and shadow. The 13 suites are palatial and private, though privacy is always relative at an unfenced lodge – a rustle outside is likely to have a heartbeat. Elephants saunter up to drink from the plunge pool, and skittish impala appear as I test the outdoor shower, prompting the peculiar, electric intimacy of holding another creature’s gaze.

The Big Five

We saw the Big Five within 24 hours. It was not my first safari, but it was my first leopard sighting: a female draped beneath a tree with the sort of molten-eyed disdain that would be intolerable in a person but magnificent in a leopard. After that came wildebeest, zebras, white rhinos, buffalo locking horns with graceless momentum, bashful warthogs bolting into the scrub, tails raised like little radio masts, and an elderly giraffe happily munching on acacia thorns. We returned daily to a coalition of lion brothers sprawled in the aftermath of a night’s hunting.

The advantage of a private reserve is the freedom to leave the marked tracks. But proximity is only half of it. The greater privilege is to have the bush translated for you. Louis, our tracker, grew up on the edge of this landscape and reads it with a sixth sense: a softened paw print, a snapped stem, a hint that something was here. He jumps down from the Land Cruiser carrying his stick, exchanging glances with Ranger Jamiel that seem to contain an entire silent language of trust. Louis heads off between burnt trees, while Jamiel drives on, providing the steady commentary of someone who’s seen this play out many times before. Moments later, we find her – a young lioness lounging in the dappled shade of a marula tree.

Their calm authority rests on deep foundations. Louis hails from a local Shangaan village and has spent decades at Sabi Sabi. The reserve’s relationship with the land is bound to the surrounding communities. Many of the staff are local, and the Sabi Sabi Foundation builds on that connection, investing in education, employment and conservation through projects including a Ranger Academy, alongside anti-poaching efforts that protect the wildlife everything here depends on.

Read more: Why South African wine is the GOAT

The spotted hyena

An hour before sunset, the 4×4 eases into a riverine thicket at the sight of elephants. A calf no bigger than a Labrador is tucked beneath her mother, slowly edging out to test the world with her trunk. We watch her in hushed fascination while Jamiel dismantles the half-baked myths we carry from childhood. The circle of life, it turns out, is not always a neat script of noble predators and hapless prey. No animal brings this home better than the safari’s most maligned criminal: the spotted hyena.

Far from a skulking scavenger, the hyena is in fact a matriarchal powerhouse. Females lead the hunt and outrank the males, with lions often opportunistic thieves stealing the hyena kills. I found them difficult to dislike, dog-curious and surprisingly tender, their rasping cackle a bonding call between friends. The Lion King owes several species a formal apology.

The reverse is equally true: Hippopotamuses, those watermelon-gobbling comedians, are among the deadliest and most territorial creatures in Africa. A young bull had recently defeated the dominant male and claimed lordship of the waterhole. His rival was a windfall for every carnivore within ten miles.

Read more: Inside South Africa’s two most exceptionally fabulous hotels

Hippo lore

Back at the lodge, hippo lore is shared over food. Tip of the day: if one charges, run in a zigzag line. Safari has a way of sharpening the appetite, and a breakfast of chakalaka, vibrant fruit, and omelettes generously loaded with biltong satisfies the ravenous elation that comes from three hours on open ground. By night, stories gather around the fire in the boma, a traditional circular enclosure historically used to protect livestock from predators, now ringed with lanterns and perfumed by smoky meats on the braai. Best of all are the sundowners, pulling over in the bush at sunset for drinks on foot. A glass of Amarula in hand, feet planted firmly on the same ground I’d seen a leopard pass that morning.

As soul-stirring as safari may be, Sabi Sabi’s newest opening suggests that it is only one facet of South Africa’s appeal. Rather than planting a flag in Cape Town’s obvious enclaves, they chose Claremont, a suburb bordering the Constantia valley, where some of the Southern Hemisphere’s oldest vineyards sit in an indecently green fold of land.

The Claremont Boutique Hotel opened in late 2025 with 15 rooms spread across a restored Cape Dutch revival manor, its gardens and pool. Built in 1928 by the pioneering female architect Magdalena Gertrude Sauer, it has a kind of romantic order that makes you feel like you’ve wandered into the house of somebody who inherited excellent taste. Veld & Vine does precisely what a suburban luxury hotel restaurant needs to do: keeps the day alive.

The bounty of South Africa

Expect excellent aged steaks, Durban bunny chows (curry-stuffed brioche, hello) and seafood from a nearby marine researcher-turned sustainable fisherman. But it is a base not a bubble, with easy access to Cafés and antique shops in Kalk Bay, once named the coolest neighbourhood in the world, and the penguin colony at Boulders Beach. Sabi guests can also book a wine safari at Klein Constantia’s iconic estate; a glass of Vin de Constance is a must. This modern revival of the sweet Muscat Constantia Wyn counted Dickens, Austen and Napoleon among its fans, the latter having thirty bottles a month shipped to St Helena during his exile.

Botanists use the term floral kingdom to describe the world’s six plant regions, categories that usually cover enormous tracts of the globe. The Cape Floral Kingdom occupies just the southwestern corner of the country but harbours an absurd concentration of life: species for species it’s fourteen times denser than the Amazon, and Table Mountain alone has more plant species than the entire UK. Head to Kirstenbosch to see these blooms in abundance. The wildlife there is no less eccentric.

In the end, my most starstruck moment was not with an apex predator, but what looked like a long-legged Furby hovering in a bush. I still have no idea what it was. Where are Jamiel and Louis when you need them?

Alan Milburn’s review on youth joblessness has urged John Healey to find billions of pounds more in spending each year on young people in order to deliver projected savings in 10 years’ time. 

Milburn’s flagship report on helping Britain’s Neets, who are young people out of employment, education and training, has said that the government must allocate £5.8bn more in public funds each year on employment opportunities by 2036. 

The report said delivering new investment “should be a priority” in next year’s Spending Review, adding to a multitude of pressures facing the Chancellor around defence funding and public sector pay increases. 

Cuts to benefits of around £3.6bn are only set to come into effect from 2036, with initial savings on welfare largely to begin after the next General Election. 

Milburn said on Tuesday morning that the government could secure some savings if legislation is passed quickly through parliament as he said “crude cuts” would lead to “more poverty, more penury” as well as higher costs on crime and housing. 

In the short term, the government faces the task of finding about £500m in funding from existing departmental budgets for investment to enable under 25-year-olds to enter the national workforce. 

Analysis in the Milburn review suggested that cumulative welfare savings between 2030 and 2036 will add up to £13.7bn. Increased tax receipts from greater employment and a 0.4 percentage point addition to GDP each year could mean the Treasury yields a net saving, under Milburn’s projections. 

However, when new spending is accounted for, taxpayers are due to save just £200m a year after a decade of new changes. 

New problem for Spending Review

The government is due to respond to recommendations in a parliamentary statement this afternoon. 

Proposals in the report could set Healey up for a challenging Spending Review as the Chancellor refused to rule out further tax rises last week to deal with a growing list of demands on public finances. 

Government figures are also tasked with winning over Labour backbenchers to push through welfare reforms. Pat McFadden, the work and pensions secretary, told MPs on Monday that the government had to “reset the system” and offer a “new settlement for young people”. 

The review also called for funding from the apprenticeship levy to be targeted as opportunities for young people. Mayors would also be accountable for delivering services that help under 25-year-old people into the world of work and also gain some of the benefits of welfare savings. 

Milburn puts spotlight on Labour’s taxes

The Blair-era health secretary’s core ambition was to reach ‘Neet zero’ in a decade’s time, bringing the rate down from a 13.4 per cent baseline to about five per cent. This would mean that 600,000 more young people were in work, education or training as currently nearly 1m people are Neets. 

An interim report in May found that the cost of the Neets crisis totalled about £125bn a year. For every £1 that was spent on employment or education opportunities, about £25 was spent on benefits. 

The report also noted the intergenerational gaps in public spending between children and pensioners, which had grown by about 170 per cent between 2004 and 2025. 

Reforms in the report include making mayors more accountable for getting young people into work, replacing the health element of Universal Credit with a new youth allowance scheme, adding mental health support and subsidising employers with a £3,000 payment if they take on Neets for at least 6 months. 

Milburn also recommended a “glide path” towards cutting employers’ National Insurance contributions by raising the threshold from £5,000 to £10,000 over several years “when fiscal conditions allow”. 

The initial cuts for employers hiring 21 to 24-year-olds should be targeted at the retail and hospitality sectors first, according to the former health secretary. 

His calls for a partial reveral of Rachel Reeves’ tax hikes bring the Labour government’s previous decisions under renewed scrutiny.

Helen Whately, the shadow work and pensions secretary, said: “Milburn is right to criticise the tax and regulation burdens Labour have imposed on businesses. But his review is too cautious on reversing that damage and too often his answer is the big and expensive hand of the state. 

“Overall, it fails to bring down the welfare bill, proposes billions more in government spending and won’t make the slightest difference for young people stuck on welfare now – because nothing will happen for at least three years.”

Modella Capital has kicked off a sale of TG Jones, the high street business that formerly traded as WH Smith, less than two years into its ownership.

The private equity firm has called in advisors at Teneo to oversee an auction of the retail business, which includes about 350 shops and 3,500 workers, in the weeks running up to Christmas. 

Modella had not been proactively seeking a deal but decided to trigger an auction after receiving unsolicited expressions of interest in buying the business, it is understood.

The process will take place in the coming weeks, but a transaction would not take place until after Christmas, in the first quarter of next year, sources close to the matter told City AM.

The group snapped up WH Smith’s 480 high street shops for an initial £10m in June last year and later pushed through a divisive restructuring plan which it claimed was necessary to ensure the retailer’s survival. The turnaround plan, opposed by landlords who objected to proposals to slash the rent paid by TG Jones, triggered the closure of up to 150 of the retailer’s sites.

Modella faced criticism for its early stewardship of the former WH Smith shops, after it rebranded each site with new TG Jones branding and charged royalties for the new moniker.

The private equity firm believes it has set the retailer back on the right course since taking over, with one person close to Modella saying it is now a “viable but smaller” business.

Joe Price, Modella’s managing director, said: “When TG Jones was acquired in 2025, it was a loss-making business with an uncertain future. Turning it around meant taking some hard decisions, including closing stores through a court-approved restructuring plan. 

“We are extremely grateful to our colleagues from across the business for their continued support. The turnaround is starting to deliver, and we are seeing improved trading results,” he added.

TG Jones sale to shake up high street

The auction of TG Jones, first reported by Sky News, will inevitably draw comparisons with the ongoing sale of Poundland, which is racing to avoid collapse after its owners, Gordon Brothers, refused bids which would have kept the discount retailer afloat.

Modella Capital is conscious of the timing, sources close to the process said, though they insisted that TG Jones is in a different position. 

The sale of Poundland has centred on a £30m loan Gordon Brothers inherited when it bought the company, which the investment firm has insisted be repaid in full. No such financial instrument would play a part in TG Jones’s auction, it is understood. 

Before Modella Capital bought its 480 shops, WH Smith had traded on UK high streets for 233 years, after being established as a newsagent by Henry Walton Smith in 1792.

Modella Capital has garnered a reputation for picking up struggling high street retailers, often putting them into administration soon after buying them. 

Claire’s Accessories and The Original Factory Shop both collapsed earlier this year after being bought by the private equity firm, though Hobbycraft, which Modella also owns, has survived its own restructuring plan.

Alex Willson, TG Jones chief executive, said: “As ever, our focus is on providing a great experience for customers, especially with the critical Christmas period coming up. 

“We continue to execute our turnaround plan, which is improving our performance month by month. We’re grateful to our fantastic colleagues for their commitment; and to our suppliers, our owner and other stakeholders for their continued support,” he added.

Twenty years after introducing one of Switzerland’s most ingenious travel-watch innovations, VOGARD returns with ENCORE – a rare opportunity to own an original created with the inventor himself.

The real engines of innovation

For all the attention lavished upon the giants of Swiss watchmaking, the industry’s most remarkable ideas often emerge from far smaller workshops. Independent watchmakers remain the guardians of genuine horological innovation, free from committees, focus groups and corporate caution.

One such example is VOGARD, a little-known but ingenious Swiss brand that developed one of the most practical world-time mechanisms ever created. The result feels almost cinematic. The first time you wear a VOGARD and change time zones, you feel less like an accountant adjusting a watch and more like James Bond preparing for departure. Simply rotate a city to the 12 o’clock position and, as if by magic, the hour hand jumps to the correct local time.

Elegant, intuitive and rather addictive.

How the VOGARD world-time mechanism works

The beauty of any great invention lies in making complexity disappear.

Beneath VOGARD’s effortless operation sits an extraordinarily sophisticated mechanism. Unusually, the watch case itself forms part of the movement. Hidden inside is a transmission system that converts the rotation of the external bezel into a precise adjustment of the internal mechanics.

More than 500 components work together with tolerances measured in hundredths of a millimetre. Such precision allows VOGARD to achieve daily accuracy deviations of no more than ten seconds. The company developed a rather charming philosophy along the way: their watches are intentionally regulated never to run slow. Better to arrive slightly early than miss a flight entirely.

Swiss punctuality, one might argue, in its purest form.

Mike Vogt: The inventor behind the idea

The mastermind behind VOGARD is Swiss watch industry veteran Mike Vogt.

Raised in Grenchen, Switzerland’s watchmaking heartland, he gained his first hands-on experience while working at Swatch as a student in 1983. His international breakthrough came during the 1990s as Marketing Director of TAG Heuer, where his famous “Don’t Crack Under Pressure” campaign helped fuel the brand’s revival.

As the executive responsible for Formula One timing, Vogt became acquainted with many of the sport’s legends, including Ayrton Senna. He would later donate a personal watch gifted to him by Senna shortly before the Brazilian driver’s tragic death, an item that found its way into TAG Heuer’s Museum.

After subsequent creative work alongside Tom Ford at Gucci and a successful venture into the emerging internet economy, Vogt finally accumulated the resources needed to pursue a lifelong dream: creating the perfect world-time watch.

A world-time watch debut that turned heads at Baselworld

That dream reached the public stage at Baselworld 2004.

Visitors accustomed to traditional world-time watches encountered something entirely different. Instead of navigating complicated pushers, crowns and instructions, users could change time zones instantly and intuitively.

The industry took notice. VOGARD had transformed what had long been considered a specialist complication into something travellers could actually enjoy using.

A surprisingly rare achievement in luxury watchmaking.

Personalising time itself

What truly brought the mechanism to life was the idea of thematic rotating bezels.

Pilots could wear official IATA airport codes.

Motorsport enthusiasts followed Formula One circuits around the globe. The Stockmaster model featured major financial indices, ensuring that ambitious CFOs could keep track of markets while crossing continents.

The brand’s slogan, “The Time of YOUR World”, was more than marketing copy.

Owners could commission entirely bespoke bezels engraved with destinations, yacht marinas, golf courses, favourite wine regions, production sites or personal memories. One customer, reportedly a ski instructor, requested a bezel engraved with the names of former romantic adventures scattered across the globe.

Possibly the first world-time watch that doubled as a confidential autobiography.

Around the world and a strategic crossroads

Between 2004 and 2014, VOGARD expanded to approximately thirty points of sale across major international cities, including London, Paris, New York, Dubai, Hong Kong and Moscow, while also establishing a presence in luxury destinations such as Aspen, Beverly Hills, Sankt Moritz and Saint-Tropez.

Success, however, created a difficult question. Should the company invest heavily in global expansion and costly boutique networks, particularly in Asia, or monetise the technology it had already proven?

In 2014, VOGARD chose the latter path, selling its patents to a respected Swiss watch group. It was a bold decision. New watch production ceased, while the company focused primarily on supporting existing collectors through after-sales service.

For many, it seemed the story had reached its final chapter.

VOGARD ENCORE: The return of the original world-time watch

Fortunately, watch enthusiasts rarely accept a good ending when a better sequel is possible.

In 2026, marking the brand’s 25th anniversary and responding to persistent demand from collectors, VOGARD secured a one-time licence to relaunch its iconic world-time concept through the new ENCORE collection.

Leading the return is the ENCORE1, featuring VOGARD’s proprietary SiTin case technology, an exceptionally hard and lightweight material that represents yet another innovation from the independent Swiss brand. Unveiled for the very first time at the London Watch Week City Edition, its distinctive metallic bronze finish and colour underscore the collection’s ambition to blend engineering excellence with contemporary elegance.

For serious collectors, ENCORE offers something money alone rarely buys: authenticity. This is not merely the revival of a respected independent watchmaker, but a rare opportunity to acquire an original VOGARD directly from the inventor who conceived the concept more than two decades ago.

While the collection includes beautifully finished watches ready to accompany their owners around the world, those seeking something even more personal can work directly with Mike Vogt to create a bespoke bezel reflecting places, achievements, memories or destinations that define their own journey.

After all, luxury is no longer about owning what everyone else has.

It is about carrying your own world on your wrist.

Imperial Brands expects to slash up to 2,500 jobs in the coming years as the tobacco giant hunts for £320m in savings.

The FTSE 100 firm revealed on Tuesday it will cut between 2,100 and 2,500 further jobs across its international operations before 2030. This follows the firm already reducing its headcount by 2,100 in the last financial year.

The group, which owns brands including JPS, Golden Virginia and Rizla, is among a number of tobacco firms to suffer from falling demand for cigarettes as consumers switch to vapes and nicotine pouches.

“Throughout this transformation, we are committed to following appropriate consultation processes and supporting our people,” the firm told shareholders. 

The Bristol-based firm saw its revenue fall by 1.5 per cent to £31.7bn in the year to September. Its operating profit dipped by 10 per cent to £3.1bn, which the group blamed in part on its cost-savings programme.

Lukas Paravicini, chief executive officer of the firm, said: “While continuing to invest in and build future consumer capabilities, underpinned by new technologies, we are confident of achieving at least £320 million of annual savings by 2030.

“We have delivered annualised savings of £90 million, with actions taken since the programme began supporting future annualised savings of £180 million – more than half of our target.”

Disruption from Russian drone strike

Imperial Brands, like rival firms including British American Tobacco, are racing to adapt to falling demand for cigarettes, as its tobacco sales slipped by 3.4 per cent in the year to September.

But the group benefitted from an 11.4 per cent uplift in takings from its “next generation products,” which include vapes and nicotine pouches.

The firm is racing to gain more share of the “smokeless” tobacco market with its acquisitions of American and Swedish nicotine pouch brands Black Buffalo and Helwit, which it said are driving its growth in the category.

Imperial Brands said its profit for the next year will be more heavily weighted towards the second half than usual, owing to the supply chain disruption caused by a Russian drone attack on its factory in Ukraine. 

The group said: “The geopolitical and macroeconomic backdrop continues to be uncertain, with the potential future impact of the Middle East conflict, on both costs and consumer behaviour, remaining difficult to assess. 

“However, the power of our brands, depth of our portfolios and diverse growth levers across our global markets mean we are well placed to navigate any future volatility.”

The youth unemployment rate far exceeded the national rate, official data has shown, just as the Alan Milburn review is expected to lay out proposals for radical cuts to welfare and new investment to help young people into work. 

The Office for National Statistics showed the unemployment rate for people aged between 16 and 24 remained above 15 per cent in the period between July and September.

This soared ahead of the general unemployment rate of 4.6 per cent, a fall from last month’s drop. The ease at the national level could make traders more cautious about the UK’s inflation outlook. The unemployment rate was at about 4.4 per cent as Labour came into power. 

There were also more redundancies in the quarter, according to new figures, while the inactivity rate eased slightly.

Vacancies dropped further below 700,000 in the three-month period as small businesses reported that higher costs stopped them from taking on more workers.

Later on Tuesday, Milburn is expected to call for a “complete system reset” on the UK’s approach to welfare and work for under 25-year-olds. 

Data published on the morning of the publication of his flagship review on young people who are not in employment, education or training (Neets) reflects the enormous difficulties the government faces in turning the jobs market around. 

‘Particularly bad’ for young people

“The latest figures provide a mixed picture overall,” said Liz McKeown, director of economic statistics at the ONS.

“The employment rate increased and the unemployment rate fell in the latest quarter, though these movements partly reflect particularly large differences in employment status between the groups entering and leaving the survey.

Annual earnings growth excluding bonuses slipped to 3.5 per cent, matching expectations for the period between July and September. Including bonuses, wage growth was at about 3.6 per cent. 

A government spokesperson said: “Despite the difficult global backdrop, the unemployment rate is falling, and the number of people in work is rising.

“We are determined to go further. Our £2.5bn youth employment support will give almost one million young people opportunities to earn and learn, while wider reforms including improving Jobcentres, will create a more personalised work and skills advice service for all.

“But we won’t be complacent and the Milburn Review will help shape our next steps for young people not in education, work or training.”

Martin Beck, chief economist at WPI Strategy, said the fall in job numbers showed the problem was not that businesses were firing workers, “it’s that they’re increasingly reluctant to hire them”.

“That is particularly bad news for young people trying to get a foot on the employment ladder, and underlines the urgency of the Milburn Review’s recommendations,” Beck said.

“It also raises further questions about the wisdom of government policies that have made employing people more expensive and potentially more burdensome, notably higher employer National Insurance contributions and expanded employment rights.”

Youth unemployment clampdown carries risks

The latest set of data and government announcements is set to be closely monitored by industry figures and City investors amid risks to public finances from higher spending and lower tax receipts. 

Ahead of the publication of the Milburn review, Resolution Foundation economist Ruth Curtice said turning around the jobs market would require “significant investment”. 

She added that there would be pressure on the government to “tread carefully” around possible benefits cuts. 

Labour market data could also influence Bank of England policymakers ahead of another possible interest rate hike this year. 

The National Institute of Economic and Social Research urged the Monetary Policy Committee to lift interest rates from four per cent to five per cent due to the risks that a stabilisation in the jobs market could send inflation spiralling over the coming months.
